title: Redefining student assessment in AI-infused learning environments: a systematic review of challenges and strategies for academic integrity
authors: Prince Daughin Ngqabutho Ncube; Godwin Pedzisai Dzvapatsva; Courage Matobobo; Memory M Ranga
source_used: Springer OA PDF from queue oa_url (link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s43681-025-00871-w.pdf); CC BY 4.0; journal pagination AI and Ethics (2026) 6:68, pp. 1-14
ft_reason: HE assessment and academic integrity under GenAI is the central focus; peer-reviewed systematic review published 2025 (issue 2026), English. Meets IC1-IC5.
study_design: Systematic review (PRISMA-guided) with inductive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke) of included empirical studies
country: South Africa / UK (author affiliations); included studies international
discipline: Higher education generally (cross-disciplinary); includes some IT/engineering education sources
level: Higher education (undergraduate and postgraduate; not separated)
sample: Scopus (20), IEEE Xplore (300) and ScienceDirect (65) = 385 records; 382 after deduplication; 118 full texts screened; 56 empirical studies included (2015-2025 window)
genai_tools: ChatGPT and GenAI tools generally; AI detection tools (Turnitin, GPTZero) and AI proctoring discussed

key_findings.finding: Six themes were grouped into two categories: challenges to integrity in unsupervised assessments (AI-enabled dishonesty, over-reliance, reliability/fairness of AI-generated work) and strategies (AI-resistant/process-based assessment, institutional policy and literacy, human-AI collaboration).
key_findings.location: Sec 3.5 p.5; Sec 4 p.6; Tables 2-4 p.7

key_findings.finding: Included studies report that conventional plagiarism tools such as Turnitin are unreliable for AI-generated text (false positives and negatives), and many institutions lack clear AI-in-assessment guidelines, leaving staff inconsistent.

The literature favours oral exams/vivas, scaffolded multi-stage submissions with drafts, reflective journals, higher-order Bloom tasks and real-world problem tasks as AI-resistant, process-focused designs.
Some universities have introduced mandatory AI-disclosure requirements and AI-literacy programmes for students and staff to promote transparency and responsible use.
AI-assisted assessment may widen inequity, since students with better access to AI tools gain an advantage.

dimensions.authenticity: Recommends authentic, application-based tasks (e.g., real-life problem-solving projects) as both more valid and harder to outsource to AI.
dimensions.capability_verification: Proposes routine oral vivas, rather than only after suspected misconduct, to confirm that students understand their own work.
dimensions.integrity_security: Synthesises evidence that AI detectors are unreliable and that unsupervised essays and take-home assignments are especially vulnerable.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Argues assessments should target higher-order Bloom levels (create/evaluate) that current GenAI handles less well.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Advocates AI-use declarations in rubrics, human-AI collaboration, and critique of AI outputs rather than outright bans.
dimensions.workload: Notes that AI-based grading promises efficiency but has reliability and fairness limits.
dimensions.feasibility: Mentions supervised, time-constrained assessment as a fallback but notes criticism that it is distant from real-world tasks.
dimensions.process_visibility: Multi-stage submissions with drafts let educators follow learning progress and students' interaction with AI over time.
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Flags the digital divide and unequal access to AI tools; suggests naming AI platforms that all learners can access.

author_recommendations: Use oral vivas routinely as part of assessment, not only to verify authenticity when misconduct is alleged (not tested)
Add sections to rubrics where students declare how they used AI (not tested)
Assess throughout the learning process (process-oriented, multi-stage assessment) rather than only the final product (not tested)
Specify which AI platforms may be used, choosing ones all learners can access, to support equity (not tested)
Institutions should adopt AI policy frameworks and provide AI-literacy and assessment-design professional development for staff (not tested)
limitations: Authors note over-reliance on literature dominated by educator voices (p.11). Other issues: only three databases; the search string required the phrase 'Academic Integrity'; no formal quality appraisal of included studies; 2015-2025 window extends before GenAI; results are not split by discipline or level.

quality.note: Clear RQ and transparent PRISMA flow with numbers. However, there was no critical appraisal of included studies, and the narrow search string and three databases limit how comprehensive it is.

title: Incorporating Generative AI into Software Development Education
authors: Olga Petrovska; Lee Clift; Faron Moller; Rebecca Pearsall
source_used: Swansea University Cronfa repository PDF (record cronfa65079; listed by OpenAlex as submittedVersion, laid out in ACM format, 4 pp.). The ACM oa_url returned a bot-check page and was not bypassed.
ft_reason: Degree apprenticeship (HE) in software engineering; designs and reports formative and summative assessments built around critical evaluation of ChatGPT output; peer-reviewed ACM conference paper (published Jan 2024; DOI dated 2023); English.
study_design: Practice/experience report: three anonymous surveys plus experimental formative and summative assessments, analysed descriptively and with a coding scheme
discipline: Software engineering / computing (Applied Software Engineering Degree Apprenticeship)
level: Undergraduate (degree apprenticeship, first-year and final-year learners)
sample: Surveys: first-year learners n=12, final-year learners n=12, industry professionals n=13; experimental summative assessment: 17 first-year learners (Professional Issues module)
genai_tools: ChatGPT

key_findings.finding: The summative assessment had learners use ChatGPT to generate Java and Pep/8 Assembly code and one-sided arguments, then critique the outputs and reflect on their prompting 'journey'. The rubric marked prompt construction, rigour of analysis and ethical discussion.

For a simple Java task, 94% of learners' first prompts produced compiling code. For Pep/8 Assembly only 29% obtained compilable code, and one learner did not notice the output was Python (an example of over-reliance).
Most learners were critical of ChatGPT's cryptocurrency-sustainability argument (76%), rising to 81% after refinement. They judged long nuanced text generation weaker than their own work.
Over 80% of all surveyed participants (learners and industry) showed some willingness for formal GenAI training. Only 2 of 13 industry respondents reported GenAI integration at their workplace.

dimensions.authenticity: Industry partners and apprentices want GenAI skills, which motivated assessments that mirror workplace use of GenAI in software engineering.
dimensions.capability_verification: Designing tasks where GenAI performs poorly (Pep/8 Assembly) exposed learners' understanding and over-reliance.
dimensions.integrity_security: Framed as assessments that use GenAI 'without the risk of the AI tools doing the homework', by marking critique rather than the output itself; not formally evaluated.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Rubric criteria (prompt quality, rigour of comparison with own work, ethical analysis) target critical evaluation outcomes.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: AI use was required and scaffolded, and learners discussed professional and ethical implications of GenAI in education and work.
dimensions.feasibility: Implemented in a real module with 17 learners; the authors plan to extend it to more modules.
dimensions.process_visibility: Learners documented and reflected on their prompting 'journey', which was marked.

author_recommendations: Embed GenAI in assessments that require learners to critically evaluate AI output against their own work (implemented descriptively; learning effect not formally tested)
Develop summative assessments that give students the choice of using GenAI tools (future work; not tested)
Provide formal GenAI training within degree apprenticeship programmes (not tested)
limitations: No explicit limitations section. Small, single-programme samples (12/12/13 survey respondents; 17 assessed learners); descriptive percentages only; self-reported time estimates; no comparison group; short 4-page practice paper.

quality.note: Clear practice aim with a reasonable descriptive design for a practice report. Samples are small but described. The authors do not acknowledge limitations.

title: The Summative Assessment of Generative AI Usage within Academic Writing in a Computing Foundation Year
authors: Tom Prickett; Carly Foster
venue: Proceedings of the 10th Computing Education Practice Conference (CEP '26), ACM
ft_reason: Computing foundation year at a UK university (HE); summative assessment design that requires and evidences GenAI use, with declaration and integrity discussion; ACM CEP practice paper (peer reviewed); 2026 proceedings; English.
study_design: Practice report (CEP 'what/why/does it work' format) describing a redesigned assessment, with end-of-module student perception survey results and module outcome data
discipline: Computing (digital society / social and professional issues module in a computing foundation year)
sample: 88 foundation-year students in one 12-week module, semester 1 2024-25; module survey had 19 responses (22%) in 24-25, compared with 19 responses (20%) in 23-24
genai_tools: Student choice of free GenAI tools; PREP & EDIT prompting framework taught; Turnitin AI checker used in marking; Claude since provided to students (future work)

key_findings.finding: Assessment 1 (80%) required GenAI use. Marks were spread over the search process, evidence of web and library search, the prompts used and AI outputs, and a reflection checking AI output for completeness, bias and hallucinations.
Each student had to pick a different technology for the individual part, making the task divergent. The authors cite this as a way to promote authenticity and reduce cheating.
In both assessments students had to declare and evidence any GenAI use. For the reflective report (20%), AI drafts had to be appended and the report personalised with module evidence.

Student satisfaction items improved on the previous year: 100% agreed or mostly agreed in 24-25, compared with 68-79% in 23-24 (n=19 each year). All students who completed every component passed; the module mean was 60% (SD 15).
No misconduct was detected by the Turnitin AI checker or manual scrutiny. The authors note that detectors give false positives and negatives and may be biased against non-native writers.

dimensions.authenticity: Argues the task is authentic because validating AI-generated content is a challenge adult citizens face (Wiggins sense), while noting authenticity alone does not protect integrity (Sec 2).
dimensions.capability_verification: Students must independently verify AI output against traditional research and show evidence of it, which the authors argue AI would find hard to produce (Sec 1.1, Sec 2).
dimensions.integrity_security: No misconduct detected via Turnitin AI checker and manual review; authors acknowledge detector limits and plan face-to-face demos/walkthroughs because written tasks are increasingly challenged (Sec 4, Sec 6).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Links tasks to QAA computing benchmark expectations for written communication and module aims on information and AI literacy (Sec 1).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: GenAI use is required in assessment 1 and encouraged in assessment 2, with explicit teaching of ethical use, prompting frameworks and misconduct avoidance (Sec 1, Sec 2).
dimensions.feasibility: Implemented in a real 88-student module with outcomes in line with institutional norms (Sec 3, Sec 4).
dimensions.process_visibility: Marks are given for the research process, prompt logs and search evidence rather than only the end product (Sec 1.1, Sec 2).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Requires that tools used are free to students; notes detector bias against non-native English speakers (Sec 1, Sec 4).

author_recommendations: Embed required, declared and evidenced GenAI use in assessed academic writing in computing programmes, with marks for evaluating AI output (tested descriptively in one module)
Use divergent individual tasks (a different topic per student) to support authenticity and reduce cheating (not tested separately)
Supplement written assessments with face-to-face demonstration or walkthrough (not tested)
Extend the approach to later degree stages and research student perceptions of AI teaching (not tested)
limitations: Single module and single cohort; low survey response (19 of 88); comparison with the previous year is descriptive only; misconduct outcome depends on AI detectors the authors themselves call unreliable; no formal limitations section. 4-page practice report.

quality.note: Clear aim and well-described context (n=88, module, assessment weights). Evaluation is thin: 22% survey response, no inferential analysis, and a misconduct claim resting on AI detection. Study limitations are not discussed.

title: Developing evaluative judgement for a time of generative artificial intelligence
authors: Margaret Bearman; Joanna Tai; Phillip Dawson; David J. Boud; Rola Ajjawi
source_used: Deakin University figshare repository (article 25720845; file bearman-developingevaluative-2024.pdf, the published version, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0). The T&F oa_url returned a bot-check page and was not bypassed.
ft_reason: Peer-reviewed conceptual paper on higher-education assessment practice for developing evaluative judgement with GenAI; English; 2024. Assessment design is the primary focus (IC2), though it concerns assessment for learning more than integrity.
study_design: Conceptual paper
discipline: Higher education generally (cross-disciplinary)
sample: not applicable (conceptual)
genai_tools: Generative AI generally (ChatGPT as example)

key_findings.finding: Proposes three intersections of evaluative judgement and GenAI: judging the quality of GenAI outputs, judging the quality of one's own GenAI processes (e.g., prompts, when to stop for ethical reasons), and using GenAI to appraise students' own evaluative judgements.

Adapts five existing assessment strategies (self-assessment, peer review, feedback, rubrics, exemplars) to each of the three intersections, e.g., peers jointly reviewing each other's GenAI processes against a rubric.
Argues evaluative judgement should be built systematically across a programme through repeated calibration against AI, peers, teachers and exemplars, including ipsative tracking over years.
Warns that GenAI corpora likely reflect Global North and dominant perspectives, so students' developing notions of quality may reproduce existing inequities.

dimensions.authenticity: Positions judging the quality of AI outputs as a capability graduates will need daily in an AI-mediated world.
dimensions.integrity_security: Little direct treatment of cheating; the approach is meant to interrupt uncritical GenAI use rather than secure assessment.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Treats evaluative judgement as a learning outcome to be developed deliberately through assessment design.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Students should learn when GenAI use is and is not acceptable, including privacy, intellectual property and task rules.
dimensions.feasibility: Builds on existing formative strategies (self/peer assessment, rubrics, exemplars) rather than new infrastructure.
dimensions.process_visibility: Proposes that students self- and peer-assess their GenAI processes (e.g., iterative prompting) as part of assessment tasks.
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Raises bias in GenAI training data (Global North, dominant knowledge) as an equity concern for developing judgement.

author_recommendations: Adapt self-assessment, peer review, feedback, rubrics and exemplars to develop judgement of GenAI outputs, processes, and AI appraisals of student judgement (not tested)
Build evaluative judgement systematically across a programme of assessment, including iterative calibration and ipsative feedback (not tested)
Teach safe and effective GenAI use through classroom dialogue; teachers can model their own limitations with intellectual candour (not tested)
limitations: Conceptual, with no empirical evaluation of the proposed strategies. Early student-use survey data cited are acknowledged as of limited generalisability. A section on 'unknowns' (future credibility of AI, corpus bias, technological change) stands in for a formal limitations statement.

quality.note: Well-grounded conceptual argument from established evaluative-judgement literature. q3 was scored N because there is no data (conceptual). There is no explicit limitations section.

title: Is AI changing learning and assessment as we know it? Evidence from a ChatGPT experiment and a conceptual framework
authors: Oluwaseun Kolade; Adebowale Owoseni; Abiodun Egbetokun
source_used: Sheffield Hallam University Research Archive (SHURA 33167; Published Version [VoR], CC BY-NC-ND). The cell.com oa_url returned a bot-check page and was not bypassed.
ft_reason: HE essay assessment validity and integrity under ChatGPT (plagiarism checks, human grading) plus a framework for AI-assisted assessment; peer-reviewed; 2024; English.
study_design: Quasi-experiment (ChatGPT-generated essays tested with Turnitin, Grammarly and two human markers) followed by a conceptual framework
discipline: Social sciences / business (Masters students)
sample: Purposive sample of Masters social-science students (reported as 20 students and 33 essay outputs in Stage 2, but 18 participants and 23 essays in Stages 1 and 4; Table 1 lists S1-S20 and E1-E33); two PhD-holding lecturers as assessors
genai_tools: ChatGPT 3.0 and 3.5 (as labelled by authors); Turnitin; Grammarly; CopyLeaks AI detector tried and dropped

key_findings.finding: Turnitin similarity was low for essays from distinct accounts (mostly under 25%). Repeat essays from the same account with the same prompt rose to 86-99%, so Turnitin was not effective for AI essays generated across multiple accounts.

Human markers rated many AI essays satisfactory to good (scores roughly 40-77.6%), but noted missing theory, case examples and citations, and judged some essays similar in substance despite low Turnitin similarity.
All citations and references ChatGPT supplied for the essay and report could not be found (placeholder or fabricated references).
key_findings.location: Sec 5 p.12; footnote 2 p.12; Table 2 p.11

key_findings.finding: The authors propose an AI-assisted assessment framework based on Miller's pyramid, extending assessment from knowledge (know what) to competence (know how) and performance (show how). It has six propositions (chatbot feedback, automated essay scoring, adaptive feedback/testing, serious games).

dimensions.authenticity: Argues assessment should move beyond essays to competence and performance in simulated real-life contexts (e.g., serious games).
dimensions.capability_verification: Shows that essays can be produced by ChatGPT at passable-to-good quality, weakening essays as evidence of individual capability.
dimensions.integrity_security: Shows Turnitin missed AI-generated essays from distinct accounts and AI detectors were imprecise; human markers spotted some content similarity.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Framework aligns assessment levels with Miller's know what / know how / show how outcomes.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Advocates accepting and supporting student AI use while restructuring assessment toward higher levels.
dimensions.scalability: Proposes automated essay scoring and adaptive testing to reduce staff time at scale (untested).
dimensions.workload: Notes that manual expert scrutiny for AI-generated work is time-consuming and adds workload.
dimensions.feasibility: Acknowledges operationalising the framework needs systemic change and may face stakeholder resistance.
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Notes work-based placements are resource-intensive and unequally available, motivating AI simulations.

author_recommendations: Use AI chatbots for formative feedback and automated essay scoring for summative knowledge assessment (not tested)
Use AI-assisted adaptive feedback and adaptive testing for competence-level assessment (not tested)
Use computer serious games for formative and summative performance assessment (not tested)
Higher education providers should embrace rather than resist AI and rethink essay-centred assessment (not tested)
limitations: Authors note: possible topic and geographic effects of the single prompt; straightforward prompts with a single run (no iteration); no comparison with student-written essays; single discipline (p.15). Further issues: inconsistent counts of participants and essays; assessors were drawn from the authors' network; the framework is not derived from or tested against the experimental data.

quality.note: Clear RQs and appropriate exploratory quasi-experiment, but the sample and essay counts are internally inconsistent (18 vs 20 participants; 23 vs 33 essays). The framework is conceptual and untested.

title: ChatGPT in the Classroom: Evaluating its Role in Fostering Critical Evaluation Skills
authors: Angela Oates; Donna M. Johnson
venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 35: 1793-1824
source_used: Springer OA PDF from queue oa_url (link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s40593-024-00452-8.pdf)
ft_reason: Master's-level HE assessment redesign where students generate an essay with ChatGPT and then critically evaluate it; examines assessment quality, marks and integrity perceptions; peer-reviewed; 2025; English.
study_design: Mixed-methods pilot: marks comparison (paired t-test vs. course averages) plus focus group and questionnaire with thematic analysis
discipline: Biomedical science (Medical Microbiology, Medical Biochemistry, Biomedical Science)
sample: 10 volunteer Master's students (4 native, 6 non-native English speakers); one ~1 h focus group; questionnaire
genai_tools: ChatGPT

key_findings.finding: ChatGPT-generated essay marks (mean 66) did not differ significantly from participants' course averages. Critical evaluation marks (mean 73) were significantly higher than course averages (paired t-test p=0.04, mean difference 9%).

AI essays had high-quality English and PEEL-style structure but lacked depth, were repetitive, and contained references that did not exist. Verifying references was the main concern in all critical evaluations.

Students preferred writing their own essays. They raised integrity concerns (AI text evading detection) and fairness concerns about paid tools, and wanted explicit guidelines and training on AI use in assessment.

Authors suggest educators use GenAI to generate materials for students to critically evaluate, and note that marks may partly reflect students' prompting skill, implying a need for new assessment criteria.

dimensions.authenticity: Critical evaluation of AI-generated content is framed as a skill valued in professional STEM and healthcare work.
dimensions.capability_verification: Marking the student's critique of the AI essay, rather than the essay itself, made students' own evaluative ability the thing being assessed.
dimensions.integrity_security: Participants saw AI-generated text as able to evade traditional integrity checks; the design embeds AI use rather than policing it.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Rubrics weighted critical analysis at 50% of the evaluation mark, matching the programme's emphasis on critical evaluation.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Orientation session covered ChatGPT limitations and integrity; students wanted explicit guidelines on acceptable AI use in assessments.
dimensions.workload: Estimated student workload 10-15 h over four weeks; cross-checking references offset AI time savings.
dimensions.feasibility: Piloted outside normal assessment with volunteers; the authors suggest AI-generated assessment content could save educator time.
dimensions.process_visibility: Students had to submit their prompts with their essay and evaluation; prompt types were analysed.
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Participants raised unequal access to paid AI tools as a fairness concern.

author_recommendations: Have educators use GenAI to generate essays, case studies or data sets for students to critically evaluate (not tested)
Add a stage where students present arguments and counter-arguments to AI for feedback (not tested)
Develop assessment criteria that account for students' interaction with AI, e.g., prompt quality (not tested)
Provide clear institutional guidelines and training on acceptable AI use in assessment (not tested)
Investigate how levels of instructional support affect students' critical use of AI (future work)
limitations: Authors note a small sample (n=10), relatively homogeneous, motivated and tech-savvy volunteers (self-selection bias), and a possible ceiling effect from high-performing students (pp.1820-1821). Further issues: no control group; comparison is with course averages and similar assessment types; the authors both designed the task and marked it.

quality.note: Clear aim and well-described context. With n=10 and a comparison against course averages rather than a control, the design is weak for causal claims. Limitations are discussed thoroughly.

title: Generative AI tools and assessment: Guidelines of the world's top-ranking universities
authors: Benjamin Luke Moorhouse; Marie Alina Yeo; Yuwei Wan
source_used: Publisher version PDF (Elsevier, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, 10 pp.) retrieved from a University of Memphis web copy (memphis.edu/publichealth/pdf-ai/education/education-teaching-article-5.pdf). ScienceDirect and the CityU Scholars repository PDF returned bot-check or 403 pages, which were not bypassed.
ft_reason: Review of HE institutional guidance on GenAI in assessment design and academic integrity; peer-reviewed; 2023; English. The authors also conceptualise GAI assessment literacy.
study_design: Document review of public institutional guidelines (rapid systematic web review) with inductive coding and descriptive statistics
country: Hong Kong / Singapore (authors); guidelines from USA (15), UK (4), Canada (2), Japan (1), Australia (1)
discipline: Higher education generally (institution-level guidance)
sample: Top 50 universities in THE World University Rankings 2023; 30 had GAI guidance; 23 university-level instructor guidelines included after criteria; extracted 15 June 2023
genai_tools: ChatGPT (57% of guidelines mention only ChatGPT); other tools e.g., DALL-E, Copilot; AI detectors (GPTZero, Turnitin)

key_findings.finding: Guidelines covered three areas: academic integrity (plagiarism, acknowledgement of GAI, detection), advice on assessment design, and communication with students (87% advised on communication).

57% of universities gave guidance on acknowledging or citing GAI use, with no standard approach. 61% mentioned detection tools, and most discouraged relying on them due to inaccuracy, privacy and trust concerns.

74% (17) gave assessment-design advice in five themes: test tasks on GAI, redesign tasks (creativity, context, authenticity, multimodal), focus on process and staged design (13 of 17), incorporate GAI into assessment, and use in-class assessment.
Some guidelines cautioned that over-reliance on in-class or oral assessments limits what students can demonstrate and may disadvantage non-native speakers and students with disabilities.
Authors propose 'GAI assessment literacy' for instructors: recognising integrity implications, designing tasks that incorporate GAI while evidencing learning, and communicating responsible use.

dimensions.authenticity: Argues that allowing GAI at stages of assessment would enhance authenticity, since GAI use will be ubiquitous in work.
dimensions.capability_verification: Reports one guideline (UCL) recommending an investigatory viva to probe authorship when AI use is suspected.
dimensions.integrity_security: Most guidelines discourage reliance on AI detectors; plagiarism definitions extended to AI-generated text and inadequate documentation.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Notes that GAI use can mean students demonstrate prompting skills rather than the targeted sub-skills, threatening validity.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Guidelines advise clear syllabus statements and open discussion of permissible use; authors argue for embracing GAI in assessment.
dimensions.scalability: Notes in-class assessment strategies may not be feasible for all classes.
dimensions.workload: Some guidelines advise balanced student workloads and longer deadlines, since time pressure is linked to improper GAI use.
dimensions.feasibility: Notes guidelines were developed rapidly and their suggestions are largely untested in practice.
dimensions.process_visibility: Guidelines recommend submitting notes, proposals, drafts, annotations and step lists, and breaking assignments into smaller pieces.
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Reports cautions that in-class or oral formats may disadvantage non-native English speakers and students needing accommodations; unequal tool access affects fairness.

author_recommendations: Institutions should develop, publish and regularly review GAI assessment guidelines (not tested)
Instructors should run assessment tasks through GAI to check how far it can complete them (not tested)
Have students use GAI as part of the assessment process and consider assessing GAI use in rubrics (not tested)
Develop instructors' GAI assessment literacy (preliminary conceptualisation, Table 7; not tested)
Adopt trust-based assessment practices and rational conversations with students about GAI implications (not tested)
limitations: Authors note: only publicly available guidelines; top-50 THE sample skews to the Global North and English-speaking institutions; only instructor-facing, university-level guidelines (p.9). Also a snapshot at June 2023, and counts differ between methods (30 found, 60%) and abstract/discussion (23, 'just under half').

quality.note: Transparent sampling frame, date and inclusion criteria; dual independent coding. The source is guidance documents, not evidence of effectiveness.

title: Chat or cheat? Academic dishonesty, risk perceptions, and ChatGPT usage in higher education students
authors: Silvia Ortiz-Bonnín; Joanna Blahopoulou
source_used: Springer OA PDF from queue oa_url (link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11218-025-10080-2.pdf); CC BY 4.0
ft_reason: Amendment 3 (redesign focus): Dishonesty and risk perceptions predicting ChatGPT use
study_design: Cross-sectional online survey; mediation analysis (GLM mediation, 10,000 bootstrap samples)
discipline: Mixed undergraduate programmes (not specified)
sample: 737 respondents; 468 ChatGPT users analysed (mean age 20, SD 4.25; 55% female); convenience sample in class, Oct-Nov 2023
genai_tools: ChatGPT

key_findings.finding: Perceived risk of ChatGPT (e.g., reliability, plagiarism accusation, privacy) was negatively associated with use frequency (beta = -0.20) and intention to use (beta = -0.46), both p<.001.
Perception of academic dishonesty (PAD) was not directly related to use frequency or intention, but had a significant indirect effect through perceived risk (indirect-only mediation).
PAD scores were high and strongly skewed (M=4.41/5, skewness -2.38), which the authors note may reflect social desirability bias.
Authors recommend universities define dishonest AI-related behaviours, set clear penalties, run ethical-use education, and adapt assessment and anti-plagiarism measures.

dimensions.integrity_security: Students who see dishonest behaviours as more serious perceive more ChatGPT risk and report less use; low detectability may weaken sanction deterrence.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Calls for consensus definitions of ethical vs. unethical AI use ('chatting' vs. 'cheating') and clear institutional guidelines.

author_recommendations: Universities should run educational programmes on responsible AI use that raise awareness of risks and clearly define dishonest behaviours and penalties (not tested)
Educators should address AI misuse in courses through anti-plagiarism measures and adapted assessment systems, including formative feedback (not tested)
Implement strategies to increase students' perception of academic dishonesty (not tested)
Future research should examine specific AI-related integrity violations longitudinally (future work)
limitations: Authors note: non-probability convenience sample from one university and no a priori power analysis; cross-sectional design (no causal inference); non-normal PAD and possible social desirability bias; general rather than behaviour-specific risk measures (p.15). Also self-reported use; AVE below 0.50 for two constructs.

quality.note: Well-reported survey with validated scales, reliability and mediation analysis. Limited relevance to assessment design: integrity attitudes only, with no assessment format evidence.

title: Adapting to AI: Innovative Approaches for Homework in Computer Science Education
authors: James Anderson; Schinnel Small
ft_reason: Undergraduate CS (introductory programming) context; homework/assignment design for integrity under AI tools is the primary focus; GenAI; FIE 2025 innovative practice work-in-progress paper (peer-reviewed conference); 2025, English. Meets IC1-IC5, although the evidence base is thin.
study_design: Innovative practice work-in-progress / experience report: informal comparison of ChatGPT-4o solutions and instructor or textbook-author solutions for two introductory Python questions, followed by assignment-design recommendations
discipline: Computer science (introductory Python programming)
level: Undergraduate (introductory programming; students with little or no prior experience)
sample: Two programming questions (one elementary, one intermediate) adapted from a Python textbook; no student participants or data
genai_tools: ChatGPT-4o (used for comparison); ChatGPT, Stable Diffusion, Meta Llama 3, Mistral AI and GPT-4o listed as examples

key_findings.finding: For both questions, the ChatGPT-4o and instructor solutions shared core features (correct output, appropriate variable names, input handling, formatted output, comments).

The authors judge the differences distinct enough to tell human from AI code: AI solutions were more robust, followed standard practice and used concepts beyond what had been taught, whereas novice code is expected to stick to taught concepts. They also note that students can prompt AI to simplify code.
They recommend making homework depend on highly specific domain knowledge from lectures (e.g. edge cases discussed only in class) so that AI tools struggle to solve it.
They also recommend ambiguous, open-ended requirements that need student choices and written justifications, so that the task cannot simply be pasted into an AI tool.
The conclusion acknowledges that detecting AI-generated code remains challenging and often impractical.

dimensions.authenticity: Example tasks draw on realistic scenarios (a customer-data GUI with messy names and addresses; a degree-progress tracker) (Sec 7-8).
dimensions.capability_verification: Tasks requiring students to justify their own choices are proposed to show student rather than AI work (not tested) (Sec 8).
dimensions.integrity_security: Motivated by integrity concerns; argues any homework can be passed to an AI tool, and that style-based detection is limited (Sec 1, Sec 5, Sec 11).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Assignments should still target the intended skills while being harder to solve with AI (Sec 6).

author_recommendations: Test assignments in AI tools to understand the responses they generate (not tested).
Embed lecture-specific, less commonly known details in homework (not tested).
Use ambiguous, open-ended requirements and ask students to justify their choices (not tested).
Build instructor awareness of what AI-generated code looks like, while recognising detection limits (not tested).
limitations: No limitations section. title: Educational Integration of ESP32 Project-Based Learning with Generative AI: Design, Implementation, and Evaluation in Two Engineering Cohorts

venue: Mexican International Conference on Computer Science (ENC) 2025, IEEE
ft_reason: Full text confirms an HE engineering module with summative assessment redesigned for GenAI (traceable prompt logs, public prototype demo 50%, individual viva 50%, peer assessment) and explicit validity framing; IEEE ENC 2025 proceedings; English.

dimensions.capability_verification: Individual viva (50%) required students to reconstruct reasoning, explain code dependencies and failures, and propose extensions (Sec II; Sec IV).
dimensions.integrity_security: Mandatory traceability plus individual oral verification were used as a dual safeguard against uncritical AI substitution (Sec II).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Built on constructive alignment, with content validity from explicit alignment of outcomes and criteria (Sec II).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: GenAI allowed as scaffolding with mandatory disclosure, justification of decisions, and progressive fading of scaffolding (Sec II; Sec IV).
dimensions.scalability: Small cohorts only; authors call for multicentre studies with larger samples (Sec V).
dimensions.feasibility: Implemented in two five-week intensive blocks using low-cost ESP32/Arduino hardware (Sec II; Sec IV).
dimensions.process_visibility: Evidence boards (planning, code versions, test and error logs) and prompt logs fed formative monitoring and summative verification (Sec II; Sec IV).

Use analytic rubrics with anchors shared from the outset, and a viva focused on reasoning and transfer (implemented)
Add non-AI or differently constrained baseline sections, multicentre samples and viva variants (e.g., surprise cases) to test sensitivity (future work)
Use peer-assessment instruments that are more sensitive at the upper range and report internal consistency (future work)

title: Can We Design AI-Resilient Programming Assessments? Reflections from a Front-End Web Development Course
authors: Chengcheng Han; Xinfeng Ye; Sathiamoorthy Manoharan
ft_reason: Third-year undergraduate course at a New Zealand university (HE); AI-resilient take-home programming assessment design and integrity; LLMs tested on the actual assignment; IEEE EDUNINE conference; 2026; English.
study_design: Case study: classroom observation of a skewed score distribution, followed by a comparative evaluation of 13 LLM variants given the same assignment prompt, with overlay tests, MOSS similarity checks and follow-up re-prompting and self-correction trials
discipline: Computing (front-end web development: HTML, CSS, SVG)

Supplying the reference logo directly improved outputs, but all still failed the overlay test. Asking models to critique and fix their own output did not fix the real problems and often added new errors.

MOSS found no similarity in AI-generated HTML or SVG, but CSS from different models was notably similar (up to 40% between DeepSeek and Qwen). AI boilerplate such as a placeholder student ID line could signal AI use.

Interviews and fully supervised tests are effective but costly to scale; the cited estimate is about 1,000 minutes for 10-minute interviews with 100 students. The authors favour tasks needing visual-spatial reasoning but warn this resistance may be short-lived.
key_findings.location: Sec II, Sec V.C, Sec VI

dimensions.capability_verification: Tasks requiring geometric decomposition separated what LLMs could produce from what students could do after classroom practice; oral interviews are noted as an effective check on authorship (Sec II, Sec IV.C).
dimensions.integrity_security: Shows that structured take-home web tasks are fully AI-completable and that similarity detection mostly fails on AI output, apart from CSS overlap and leftover boilerplate (Sec IV, Sec V.C).
dimensions.lo_alignment: The logo task targets geometric decomposition with higher-level primitives; polygon tracing meets the visual requirement but not the learning intent (Sec IV.C).
dimensions.scalability: Supervised tests and interviews are effective but resource-intensive and hard to scale to large cohorts (Sec II, Sec V.C).
dimensions.workload: Cites about 1,000 minutes of instructor time for 10-minute interviews with 100 students; supervised tests need invigilation, facilities and timetabling (Sec II, Sec V.C).
dimensions.feasibility: Proposes redesigning take-home tasks around visual and integrative reasoning as a more practical option than eliminating take-home work (Sec V.C).
dimensions.process_visibility: Recommends iterative project reviews and tasks foregrounding intermediate representations or explainable design processes (Abstract, Sec VII).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Notes heavy reliance on high-stakes supervised testing can cause stress and limit creativity and reflection (Sec V.C).

author_recommendations: Include visual-spatial or geometric reasoning tasks in take-home assignments to resist AI completion (tested only against LLMs, not students)
Combine supervised evaluations, iterative project reviews and hands-on tasks; increase the weight of supervised assessment (not tested)
Use MOSS on CSS files and look for AI boilerplate as signals of AI use (not tested as an integrity process)
Treat AI-resilient designs as adaptive and re-check them as models improve (not tested)
limitations: The student observation is anecdotal and no student score data are presented. One prompt and one run per model. The authors judged outputs themselves, with no rubric scores or inter-rater check. Table I omits some listed models. The initial logo failures were partly caused by models being unable to fetch a linked file. Results are a snapshot in time (acknowledged).

quality.note: Clear aim and well-specified LLM testing procedure (models, dates, prompts). The motivating student evidence is not reported. Single-run testing; limitations section acknowledges temporal validity.

title: A scoping review on how generative artificial intelligence transforms assessment in higher education

ft_reason: HE context; assessment transformation and academic integrity under GenAI is the primary focus; peer-reviewed scoping review (2024, English).

key_findings.location: pp. 8-9, Sec 'More diverse and innovative assessment'

key_findings.finding: Short-term mitigations reported in the literature include oral presentations, in-person exams, projects and laboratory work, since face-to-face knowledge-based assessment was seen as not threatened by ChatGPT.

key_findings.location: pp. 7-10, Fig. 4; Sec 'Balancing GenAI and human assessment'

key_findings.finding: At institution level, assessment policies need redesign, including clear GenAI usage rules; transparent disclosure of tool use may mean use is not treated as plagiarism.

dimensions.authenticity: Reports calls for authentic, higher-order and case-based tasks that are hard for AI to replicate (pp. 9-10).
dimensions.capability_verification: Reports that ChatGPT passes many exams and essays, undermining traditional tasks as evidence of student learning (p. 7, p. 13).
dimensions.integrity_security: Integrity is the main student-level challenge (54% of articles); in-person and oral formats are proposed as more secure (pp. 7, 13).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Argues critical thinking, problem solving, creativity and AI/digital literacy should be explicit learning outcomes and assessed (p. 9, p. 14).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Recommends balancing AI-assisted and human assessment and clear institutional rules on GenAI use (pp. 10-11).
dimensions.workload: Notes assessment was historically manual and time-intensive and that GenAI may provide immediate feedback (pp. 2, 5-6); no workload data.
dimensions.feasibility: Calls for teacher professional development in assessment and AI literacy as a precondition for change (p. 14).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Notes possible bias in GenAI feedback and the need for equitable AI access (pp. 2, 6).

author_recommendations: Provide teacher professional development on assessment, AI and digital literacy (not tested).
Strengthen teacher beliefs about combining human and AI assessment, moving to mixed methods (not tested).
Institutions should review assessment policies, diversify assessment beyond exams and essays, and offer more interdisciplinary programmes (not tested).
Future research on discipline-tailored assessment strategies and standardised assessment policy (not tested).
limitations: Authors note that, as a scoping review, it cannot give specific recommendations and that many included studies discussed GenAI generically without naming technologies (p. 17). Most included studies date from 2023; there was a single search date (30 Sep 2023) and no quality appraisal of the included studies is reported.

title: The Artificial Intelligence Assessment Scale (AIAS): A Framework for Ethical Integration of Generative AI in Educational Assessment
authors: Mike Perkins; Leon Furze; Jasper Roe; Jason Alexander MacVaugh
venue: Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice
source_used: Publisher OA PDF (JUTLP) via https://open-publishing.org/journals/index.php/jutlp/article/download/810/769; saved as pdfs/R10.pdf
ft_reason: Formal framework paper for GenAI in HE assessment and integrity, peer-reviewed journal (2024, English).
study_design: Conceptual framework paper (AI Assessment Scale) grounded in a literature review
discipline: Discipline-agnostic (HE generally; notes it is applicable to K-12)
sample: Not applicable (no empirical data; the scale had only been piloted in one cohort, with no reported results)
genai_tools: GenAI generally (ChatGPT, GPT-4, image generation tools)

Recommends that Level 1 (No AI) tasks be supervised or low-stakes formative, because unsupervised no-AI conditions raise equity concerns and AI use may be undetectable; examples include viva voce and technology-free oral discussion.
At Level 3, students submit their original work alongside the AI-edited version, and at Level 4 any AI-created content must be cited; Level 3 is framed as a transitional stop-gap.

key_findings.location: pp. 11-12, Sec 'Balancing Skill Development, Engagement, and Ethics'

dimensions.authenticity: Higher levels (L4-L5) are linked to authentic and industry-style tasks that reflect professional AI use (pp. 5, 10).
dimensions.capability_verification: Level 1 under supervision, including viva voce, is the route to verify unaided knowledge and skills (p. 8).
dimensions.integrity_security: Acknowledges the scale does not stop students disguising AI use and that detection tools are flawed (pp. 4, 12).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Educators choose the AIAS level according to the learning outcomes being addressed (abstract; p. 12).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: The core contribution: graded, cumulative levels that tell students where GenAI use is permitted (pp. 6-10).
dimensions.scalability: Presented as simple and quick to implement at institutional level and adaptable to local policy (pp. 1, 7).
dimensions.feasibility: Recommends supporting guidelines and multimedia material and notes the scale must be continually updated as tools evolve (pp. 8, 12).
dimensions.process_visibility: Level 3 requires the original work in an appendix and Level 4 requires citing AI content, which makes the process partly visible (pp. 7, 9-10).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Unequal access to premium tools and to language fluency is a key concern; suggests standardising permitted tools (pp. 8, 11-13).

author_recommendations: Adopt the five-level AIAS and tailor it to institutional policy (not tested).
Run Level 1 (No AI) tasks under supervision or as low-stakes formative tasks (not tested).
Develop student-facing guidelines on ethics, citation and limitations of GenAI (not tested).
Handle GenAI misuse through assessment rubrics rather than as an academic integrity breach (not tested).
Conduct empirical studies of the AIAS in diverse settings (not tested).

title: Beyond Detection: Redesigning Authentic Assessment in an AI-Mediated World
authors: Steven Kickbusch; Kevin Ashford-Rowe; Andrew Kemp; Jennifer Boreland; Henk Huijser
ft_reason: Full text confirms HE authentic-assessment redesign for GenAI with an integrity-by-design stance; conceptual, design-led paper in a peer-reviewed journal (Education Sciences, 2025, English). Meets IC1-IC5.
study_design: Conceptual, design-led paper: integrative review, analysis of cross-disciplinary exemplars and sector guidance (QAA, TEQSA), and iterative practitioner critique, producing design patterns
discipline: Discipline-agnostic; illustrative examples for engineering and design, education, creative industries, healthcare, business and finance
level: Higher education (program-level progression from early units to capstones)
sample: Not applicable (conceptual; no new data, per Data Availability Statement)
genai_tools: ChatGPT, DALL-E, MS Copilot, GitHub Copilot (GenAI generally)

key_findings.finding: Core proposition: in an AI-mediated world authenticity is achieved through design rather than detection, via process transparency, critical/ethical AI use and assessable judgement; detection is treated as a limited, situational tool because of accuracy, bias and trust problems.

Authenticity is reconceptualised along four dimensions (task-context alignment, professional judgement and ethics, process visibility, appropriate tool use within human decision-making), treated as a continuum and staged by year level.
Discipline examples centre on students critiquing AI outputs, e.g., evaluating AI lesson plans, appraising AI clinical suggestions, interrogating AI-generated market analyses.

Transparency strategies: process logs and AI prompt records submitted with the product, reflective commentaries with explicit criteria, oral defences/annotated portfolios/recorded walkthroughs, and self- and peer critique, with a progressive release of complexity across a program.

Implementation challenges are equity of access (institutionally provided AI recommended), ethics and privacy (PIA/DPIA, tool vetting, standard prompt-log conventions), assessment load (embed process evidence in existing tasks rather than adding tasks) and staff development.

dimensions.authenticity: Authenticity is redefined as constructed in AI-present contexts that mirror professional knowledge work, as a multidimensional continuum (Sec 3, 4.1).
dimensions.capability_verification: Oral defences, annotated portfolios and recorded walkthroughs are proposed to probe reasoning and ensure work represents the student's understanding (Sec 4.3).
dimensions.integrity_security: Integrity is anchored in design rather than detection; detection is limited by error rates and bias against non-native writers (Sec 3.1).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Tool use should be purposeful and aligned with intended learning outcomes; authenticity is stage-appropriate across a program (Sec 3.2, 4.1, 4.3).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: AI is positioned as an expected, declared and scrutinised collaborator; assess how effectively and transparently students mobilise it (Sec 3.1, 4.1).
dimensions.scalability: Acknowledges process logs, reflections and oral defences can be impractical in large cohorts (Sec 5.3).
dimensions.workload: Recommends embedding transparency requirements into existing tasks and institutional recognition of assessment workload (Sec 5.3).
dimensions.feasibility: Patterns were selected to be generally feasible under typical HE constraints, though not evaluated (Sec 1).
dimensions.process_visibility: Process logs, prompt records, drafts and reflective commentaries are central evidence of learning (Sec 3.4, 4.3).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Discusses unequal access to AI, disability and linguistic diversity, and new barriers from authentic formats; recommends institutional access and accessible alternatives (Sec 5.1).

author_recommendations: Design tasks requiring students to critique, adapt and verify AI outputs (not tested)
Require process logs and AI prompt records alongside final outputs, with standardised prompt-log conventions (not tested)
Use reflective commentaries with explicit criteria, and oral defences, annotated portfolios or recorded walkthroughs (not tested)
Build authenticity progressively across a program, from transparency artefacts and short orals early to stakeholder-facing capstones (not tested)
Institutions should provide equitable AI access, complete privacy impact assessments and vet tools (not tested)
limitations: Conceptual; the pattern set is intentionally compact and non-exhaustive and has not been empirically evaluated (Sec 1). Authors call for research on discipline-specific implementations, student experience and impact on learning (Sec 6). No new data.

quality.note: Full text read. Clear proposition; derivation method stated (integrative review, exemplars, practitioner critique) and well cited; conceptual, so no data (q3 N); acknowledges the patterns are untested and non-exhaustive.

title: AI in action: Changes to student perceptions when using generative artificial intelligence for the creation of a multimedia project-based assessment
authors: Kellie A. Charles; Arsalan Yousuf; Han Chow Chua; Slade T. Matthews; Joanna Harnett; Tina Hinton

study_design: Exploratory qualitative case study (constructivist paradigm) of one unit; abductive thematic analysis of routinely collected LMS data (pre-semester Padlet posts and group project logbooks) using Messeri and Crockett's four AI personas; frequencies of personas reported
discipline: Pharmacology (capstone interdisciplinary research unit PCOL3888, Bachelor of Science)
sample: 40 enrolled students contributed Padlet posts (4355 words; 71 persona descriptions); 2 withdrew, leaving 38 students in 5 project groups of 7-8; 14 AI use cases from the logbooks of 4 groups (one group reported no AI use); semester 2, 2023
genai_tools: ChatGPT (most used, by four groups), OpenAI DALL-E 3, TikTok AI voice tool

key_findings.finding: AI use was permitted in all assessments except reflections, provided students acknowledged the tools and described their prompts and how outputs were integrated; the group logbook recorded roles, meetings, decisions and AI use.
Before the projects, students mostly saw AI in a tutor-like Arbiter role (49%), then Oracle (41%) and Quant (10%); 70% described two or more roles and none described AI as a Surrogate.

Actual use was low to moderate and confined mainly to idea generation (Oracle, 12 of 14 cases, 86%) and data analysis (Quant, 2 cases, 14%); no group used AI as an Arbiter or to write text for the final submission.

All projects reached distinction or above (over 85%) and were submitted with AI acknowledgements, but only one group fully documented prompts and outputs with evidence of evaluative judgement; two groups did so only partially.

The authors attribute the gap between perceived and actual use to student uncertainty, including conflicting messages from other units equating AI use with plagiarism, and call for assessing the learning process and students' evaluative judgement of AI outputs.

dimensions.integrity_security: Authors argue that clear guidance on assessing AI-supported process is needed to protect assessment integrity, and that bans, detectors or full return to invigilated tasks are not feasible for large science units (Abstract, Sec 4).

dimensions.feasibility: Supervisors had limited AI know-how, so no guidance on specific tools or teaching on how to use them was given (Sec 2.1).
dimensions.process_visibility: Logbooks with AI-use descriptions made the process visible, but documentation quality varied, with only one group fully detailing inputs, outputs and judgements (Sec 2.3.2, Sec 3.3).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Notes that students more confident in academic writing, including native speakers, may be less likely to use AI (Sec 4).

Assess the learning process and students' evaluative judgement of AI outputs, not just the product (not tested).
Provide clear guidance to educators and students on assessing AI-supported learning (not tested).
Expand professional development in AI literacy for educators and share exemplars of AI integration (not tested).
limitations: Authors acknowledge: a small cohort of final-year science students in one specialised unit; few AI use cases; findings may reflect the early stage of AI tools in late 2023 (Sec 4.1). dimensions.lo_alignment: Assessment criteria (comprehension, analysis, critical evaluation, writing) mapped to Bloom's and Driscoll's models (pp. 3-4, Fig. 3).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: School policy lets lecturers forbid, authorise or encourage GenAI; this module encouraged it (p. 2, p. 3).
dimensions.process_visibility: Prompts and conversations appended to submissions gave assessors evidence of the process (p. 3).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Notes concern about free versus paid GenAI access and disadvantage for students with weaker language skills (p. 9).

author_recommendations: Avoid or broaden lists of example tools in assignment briefs to reduce performative claims (not tested).
Use more directive brief language to encourage interpretive reflection (not tested).
Consider providing GenAI-generated model answers that students must exceed (not tested).
Develop programme-level synoptic assessments and test language proficiency independently (not tested).
Develop institutional AI strategies, AI literacy and staff professional development (not tested).
limitations: Authors note students may have written what they thought assessors wanted to hear, findings are context-specific (pre-experience Master's students, one UK business school, end-of-year timing with possible assessment fatigue) (p. 12, Sec 6). The single cross-sectional cohort limits replicability (p. 5, Sec 2.4).
