title: The impact of generative AI on academic integrity of authentic assessments within a higher education context
authors: Alexander Kofinas; Crystal Han‐Huei Tsay; David Pike
ft_reason: Two UK universities (undergraduate business programmes); academic integrity of authentic assessments and GenAI detection in marking is the primary focus; GenAI (ChatGPT 3.5); peer-reviewed BJET article; 2025, English. Meets IC1-IC5 on full text.
study_design: Exploratory two-phase within-subjects experiment (blind marking of human-authored, GenAI-modified and GenAI-generated scripts, then pair reconciliation) with descriptive statistics, followed by semi-structured interviews analysed thematically (mixed methods)
discipline: Business studies (BSc Business Management; BA Business Purchasing and Supply Chain Management)
sample: 8 academic markers in 4 pairs (3-15 years HE experience); per institution 21 writing samples (three levels, each with 3 original student scripts at three grade bands, 3 GenAI-modified versions and 1 GenAI-generated script); six assessments mapped for authenticity using Hobbins et al. (2022) and Kaider et al. (2017); four interviews of about 2 hours
genai_tools: ChatGPT 3.5

key_findings.finding: Pairs' accuracy in identifying which scripts involved GenAI ranged from 33.3% (7 of 21) to 85.7% (18 of 21); the most accurate pair included the module leader, who relied on familiarity with students' writing styles.
Markers' suspicion produced six false positives on original student work and seven false negatives on GenAI-modified or GenAI-generated work.

GenAI modification raised marks mainly in the 50-59 band (9 of 12 cases, by 2-8 points), while originally first-class scripts were often marked down, suggesting markers penalised work they saw as too perfect.
Six GenAI-generated scripts, each produced in 90 minutes or less by researchers acting as a 'mischievous' student, received upper-second marks (55-70).
Differences in assessment authenticity made very little difference to detecting GenAI use, so the authors conclude that authentic assessment alone is not a safeguard.

dimensions.authenticity: Assessments ranging from low to moderate/high authenticity were all easily reproduced or modified with GenAI; more authentic tasks are also more complex and time-consuming to run (Methodology, Tables 1-2; Discussion).
dimensions.capability_verification: Argues that written, asynchronous outputs are no longer reliable indicators of learning and that performative, synchronous interpersonal assessments are needed (Conclusions).
dimensions.integrity_security: Markers could not reliably detect GenAI input, and suspicion led to both false positives and false negatives (Results, Tables 4-5).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Discusses constructive alignment and backwash as the basis for assessment design (Literature review).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Suggests GenAI could be used intentionally in assessment, for example to simulate professional environments or give iterative feedback (not tested) (Conclusions).
dimensions.scalability: Notes that highly authentic assessments are harder to manage with high student volumes (Discussion).
dimensions.workload: Notes that guidance requiring orals for every high AI-detection score would make marking far more onerous (Discussion).
dimensions.process_visibility: Recommends shifting from assessing outputs to assessing process and workplace relevance (Practitioner notes; Conclusions).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Honest students may be penalised on suspicion alone, which raises a fairness concern (Results).

author_recommendations: Give more critical attention to assessment design rather than relying on authenticity alone (not tested).
Shift towards performative, synchronous interpersonal assessments such as interactive orals and role-plays (not tested).
Assess process and socially situated knowledge application rather than written outputs (not tested).
Use GenAI intentionally in assessment design, for example to simulate professional scenarios (not tested).
limitations: Authors acknowledge the experiment was exploratory with a small sample (Conclusions), and that markers' detection cues (e.g. disjointedness due to ChatGPT 3.5 limits) may not hold for newer models (Discussion). Also noted: convenience sampling at the authors' own institutions; markers knew some scripts involved GenAI, which may have biased marking; no third marker; descriptive statistics only; the RQ3 conclusion is not broken down by authenticity level in the tables.

quality.note: Re-appraised on full text. Clear RQs, appropriate exploratory design and well-described sample and materials. q4 Unclear because conclusions (especially RQ3 on authenticity) rest on descriptive counts from 8 markers without a per-authenticity analysis. Limitations are acknowledged only briefly.

title: The rapid rise of generative AI and its implications for academic integrity: Students’ perceptions and use of chatbots for assistance with assessments
authors: Jan Henrik Gruenhagen; Peter M. Sinclair; Julie‐Anne Carroll; Philip Baker; Ann Wilson; Daniel Demant
source_used: UTS OPUS repository PDF (CC BY), http://hdl.handle.net/10453/179913; saved as pdfs/R57.pdf
ft_reason: HE students' use of GenAI chatbots for assessments and perceptions of academic integrity, with implications for assessment design; peer-reviewed (2024, English).
study_design: Cross-sectional online survey (correlational), with a supplementary thematic analysis of open-ended responses
discipline: Multi-disciplinary (includes Computer and Information Systems, Business, Health, Engineering and others)
sample: N = 337 Australian coursework students (April-June 2023); 78 gave qualitative comments
genai_tools: AI chatbots, e.g. ChatGPT

key_findings.finding: 79.5% had used a chatbot for some learning-related purpose, and 36.5% had used one for assistance with an assessment.

Of students reporting assessment use, 27.0% used chatbots to find information, 20.5% to analyse a topic, 17.8% to provide example writing for part or all of an assessment and 7.1% to solve a multiple-choice quiz.
Students gave low agreement that chatbot use is always an academic integrity breach (mean 3.6/10); students who had used chatbots for assessment agreed significantly less (2.5 vs 4.3).
Neither logistic regression model was significant overall; no psychosocial or demographic factor predicted chatbot use for assessments.
Only 33.5% had discussed chatbots with teachers versus 60.5% with peers; qualitative themes included levelling the playing field for neurodivergent and ESL students and concerns about over-reliance.

dimensions.authenticity: Argues GenAI is an opportunity to reimagine assessment as more authentic and less reliant on written knowledge recall (p. 8, Sec 5).
dimensions.integrity_security: Students commonly do not see chatbot use as cheating; authors warn a retreat to invigilated tasks may reduce authenticity (pp. 6, 8).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Recommends clear policies and co-designed codes of conduct on ethical GenAI use (p. 8, Sec 5-5.1).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Students reported chatbots supporting those with ADHD, autism, anxiety or ESL, while others raised fairness concerns about unequal access (pp. 6-7, Sec 4.5.1, 4.5.4).

author_recommendations: Define clear institutional policies and guidelines for ethical GenAI use in assessments (not tested).
Rethink assessment design towards authentic, real-world tasks rather than relying on invigilation (not tested).
Co-design codes of conduct with students and student unions, and run AI literacy campaigns (not tested).
Integrate critical evaluation of AI output and hands-on GenAI use into curricula (not tested).
limitations: Authors note a non-representative convenience sample with limited generalisability, Australia-only data, a cross-sectional design with no causal inference, and qualitative data limited to brief open-ended comments (p. 8, Sec 5.2).

quality.note: Clear RQs, validated scales with reported reliability, Bonferroni-adjusted analyses, limitations stated. Self-selected sample.

title: Toward Human-AI Collaboration: A Recommender System to Support CS1 Instructors to Select Problems for Assignments and Exams
authors: Filipe Dwan Pereira; Luiz Rodrigues; Marcelo Henrique Oliveira Henklain; Hermino Barbosa de Freitas Júnior; David Fernandes Oliveira; Alexandra Ioana Cristea; Leandro Silva Galvão de Carvalho; Seiji Isotani; Aileen Benedict; Mohsen Dorodchi; Elaine Oliveira
ft_reason: Pre-GenAI (2022) AI recommender; no generative AI context. Excluded for consistency with the currency rule applied to the CS1QA dataset; cited as background only.
study_design: Design and evaluation of an AI recommender system: data-driven effort modelling plus CNN topic classifier, evaluated in a single-blind, counterbalanced experiment with CS1 instructors against a state-of-the-art baseline (binomial multilevel regression)
country: Brazil (data from Federal University of Amazonas; instructors from Brazilian universities)
discipline: Computer science (CS1 introductory programming, Python)
sample: IDE log data from 2714 students (2016-1 to 2019-2) on 1026 distinct CodeBench problems; 35 CS1 instructors in the blind evaluation (5 groups of 7; 1 excluded for acquiescence); 210 problem pairs rated; 5-instructor think-aloud pilot
genai_tools: Not GenAI; CNN text classifier (NLP on problem descriptions, F1 0.90) with fine-grained effort features, truncated SVD and cosine nearest-neighbour recommendation

key_findings.finding: At UFAM, instructors make many variants of each computer-based assignment and on-campus exam to reduce plagiarism. Choosing equivalent problems by topic and effort is slow and depends on expert judgement.
Instructors judged 87.6% of problems recommended by the method as interchangeable with the target problem, against about 38% for the baseline (p = 1.66e-10).

The method also beat the baseline on equivalence of coding effort (81.0% vs 32.4%), resolution time (82.4% vs 50.5%), hit rate (79.1% vs 44.7%) and topic (92% vs 48%). All differences were significant.

The authors argue that a large enough pool could give each student a different but equivalent assignment or exam, discouraging plagiarism. Instructors stay in the loop to validate and correct recommendations.

dimensions.capability_verification: Proposes using equivalent-problem pools to expose fragile learning when students cannot solve an equivalent problem (Sec VII.B, not tested).
dimensions.integrity_security: Generating equivalent assessment variants (potentially one per student) is presented as a proactive plagiarism-mitigation measure (Sec III.A, Sec IX).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Equivalence is defined by CS1 syllabus topic plus effort so variants assess the same content at similar difficulty (Sec IV).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Human-AI collaboration: AI proposes problems, instructor validates and can relabel to improve the model (Sec IV, Sec IX).
dimensions.scalability: Designed for large CS1 classes using POJs; cold-start limits use on new problems without student log data (Sec I, Sec VIII).
dimensions.workload: Aims to cut the time-consuming, high-cognitive-load task of selecting problems for variants (Sec I).
dimensions.feasibility: Requires a POJ with fine-grained IDE logging and an annotated problem bank (Sec III, Sec VIII).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Variants are intended to be fair to all students regardless of which version they receive (Sec I).

author_recommendations: Use effort-and-topic-based AI recommendations to compose equivalent or personalised assignment/exam variants (tested with instructor ratings, not with students)
Create per-student assessments from a large equivalent-problem pool to discourage plagiarism (not tested)
Use equivalent-problem pools for testing-effect practice, detecting fragile learning, and pre/post tests in research (not tested)
Let instructors relabel topics and reward or penalise recommendations to improve the AI (not tested)
limitations: 35 instructors; each problem pair rated by only one instructor (no inter-rater agreement); seven variants per topic only; no evaluation with students or of actual plagiarism reduction; single institution's problem bank and data; cold-start for new problems; contribution of effort features apart from topic detection not isolated. Pre-GenAI; addresses plagiarism generally, not AI misuse.

quality.note: Explicit RQ and hypothesis, blind counterbalanced design with a pilot, appropriate multilevel analysis, detailed data description, and a substantive limitations section. Relevance to GenAI-era integrity is indirect.

title: Redefining Undergraduate Computing Education with GenAI-Facilitated Authentic In-Term Assessment
authors: Anum Masood; Vindya Wijeratne; Atm S. Alam
venue: IEEE International Conference on Teaching, Assessment, and Learning for Engineering
ft_reason: Undergraduate programming module in transnational education; design of a GenAI-permitted assessment (prompt submission, reflection, individual viva) is a substantial focus; GenAI; IEEE TALE 2025 peer-reviewed conference; 2025, English. Meets IC1-IC5 on full text.
study_design: Practice report / single-module case study: GenAI-permitted group mini-project assessed by report, code and individual viva; descriptive analysis of marks, student reflections and a usefulness survey; end-of-module quantitative survey pending
country: UK institution (Queen Mary University of London) delivering TNE programmes on two campuses in China
discipline: Introductory Java programming within BSc Engineering programmes (Digital Media Technology, Electronic Information Engineering, Intelligent Science and Technology, Telecommunications, IoT)
sample: Over 750 students across two TNE programmes, in self-formed groups (3-5 students); 8-week mini-project; numbers of reflections and survey respondents not reported
genai_tools: GenAI tools generally (ChatGPT discussed; specific tools used by students not reported)

key_findings.finding: GenAI was allowed for code generation, debugging, concepts and documentation (but not individual reflections); each group had to submit its three best prompts with justifications, and the reflection asked each student to describe their GenAI use.

Each student had a 10-minute individual viva in which they explained code and design decisions and responded to real-time modification requests; students in the same group with a well-written report sometimes received clearly different marks based on the viva.
Mark-review requests fell to around 10, which the authors describe as a substantial reduction from previous years (earlier figures not reported); they attribute this to clearer expectations.

Most students found GenAI helpful, but about 7% did not, and some students could not complete the project despite using GenAI; outcomes were not compared with earlier cohorts because the project was previously individual.
Claims that the design improved critical thinking and programming understanding are interpretive; the quantitative survey analysis was still pending.

dimensions.authenticity: Students built a Java GUI maths-learning tool for Key Stage 2-3 learners, with selected apps to be trialled by a partner school (Sec II-III, Sec IV).
dimensions.capability_verification: The individual viva with live code modifications was used to verify each student's contribution and understanding within group work (Sec III-B, Sec IV).
dimensions.integrity_security: Notes that unclear GenAI policies challenge academic integrity; the design relies on viva verification rather than detection (Sec IV).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Guidance gave acceptable and unacceptable prompt examples, and prompts were to support rather than outsource the task (Sec III-A).
dimensions.scalability: Implemented with over 750 students across two campuses using 10-minute individual vivas (Sec II).
dimensions.feasibility: Structured guidance and support were associated with consistent engagement across campuses in the TNE context (Sec IV).
dimensions.process_visibility: Submitted prompts with justifications and individual reflections expose part of the AI-assisted process (Sec III-A, Sec III-B).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Students were also required to design interfaces accessible to colour-blind children (Sec II).

author_recommendations: Combine permitted GenAI use with prompt submission, justification, reflection and an individual viva (implemented; evaluated only descriptively).
Extend the approach to other computing modules such as databases (not tested).
Teach AI literacy beyond technical skill, including fact-checking AI output and professional ethics (not tested).
limitations: Authors note no comparison with previous years and that the anonymous survey could not be linked to performance; quantitative survey analysis was pending (Sec IV). Also noted: no analysis method described for reflections; respondent numbers not reported; claims of improved critical thinking lack direct measures.

quality.note: Re-appraised on full text. RQs are stated, but data collection and analysis are only loosely described; the critical-thinking and understanding claims are not supported by data presented; some limitations are acknowledged.

title: Beyond the ban: A theoretical framework for integrating Generative AI in assessment
authors: Beth L. Chapman; Barney Dalgarno
ft_reason: Full text confirms a theoretical governance and assessment-design framework for GenAI in university assessment and integrity; peer-reviewed journal (Policy Futures in Education; online 2025, issue 2026); English. Some grounding draws on school-sector policy, but the framing is university assessment.
study_design: Theoretical/conceptual framework paper (narrative literature synthesis)
country: Australia (University of Canberra); framework references Australian policy (TEQSA, AQF, Australian Framework for GenAI in Schools)
discipline: Discipline-agnostic (university assessment; draws on school-sector literature)
sample: Not applicable (conceptual)
genai_tools: GenAI generally (ChatGPT named)

key_findings.finding: Bans on GenAI proved unenforceable and pushed use underground; detection tools are unreliable and biased; the authors treat integrity as a design problem rather than a matter of surveillance.
key_findings.location: Sections 'The initial response' and 'Academic dishonesty in the age of AI'

key_findings.finding: Cheating rates and drivers have been historically stable, so GenAI amplifies existing vulnerabilities rather than creating a new crisis; responses should target the drivers and assessment design.

A tiered governance model (government, institution, classroom/students) specifies levers: GenAI expectations in TEQSA/AQF standards, GenAI Use Statements in unit outlines, revised integrity procedures, moderation, 'GenAI readiness' accreditation checks, analytics dashboards, task-brief guidance, assessment declarations and reflective portfolios.
key_findings.location: Section 'The future of learning and assessment'; Figure 1

key_findings.finding: The Swiss-cheese model is adapted so that policy, institutional processes, assessment design and pedagogical/learner practices act as layered safeguards; alignment across layers offsets the weaknesses of any single layer.

The body gives three design principles (cognitive demand, evidence provenance such as prompt logs and drafts, transparency of AI affordances). The abstract's patterns (oral defence with artefact trail, cohort-specific data briefs, constrained-tools practicals) are not developed in the body, and oral exams and simulations appear only as future research for real-time professions.
key_findings.location: Section 'The future of learning and assessment'; Conclusion

dimensions.authenticity: Authentic assessment is called the most robust integrity mechanism but insufficient without systemic alignment; AI permission should be calibrated to whether professionals will use AI (Figure 2 text; Conclusion).
dimensions.capability_verification: Notes heavy AI reliance in assessment could leave graduates in real-time professions (teaching, healthcare) underprepared; suggests oral exams and simulations as future research (Conclusion).
dimensions.integrity_security: Layered Swiss-cheese safeguards and distributed responsibility replace surveillance; warns that a return to invigilated pen-and-paper exams risks narrowing what is assessed (Figure 2; 'Academic dishonesty in the age of AI').
dimensions.lo_alignment: Classroom-level educators should implement AI-enhanced assessments tailored to their learning outcomes (Conclusion).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Transparency of AI affordances in task briefs and rubrics, distinguishing educational from professional AI use (Figure 1 text; design principles).
dimensions.scalability: Claims the pathway is feasible at scale through governance levers, without evidence (Abstract).
dimensions.feasibility: Names concrete levers (use statements, moderation, accreditation checks, professional development, shared task banks) but does not test them (Figure 1 text).
dimensions.process_visibility: Evidence provenance via prompt logs, draft portfolios and reflective portfolios is a core design principle (design principles; Figure 2 text).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Notes unequal access to GenAI may widen inequalities and that detectors are biased against some groups (Introduction; 'Academic dishonesty in the age of AI').

author_recommendations: Adopt a tiered governance model linking national policy, institutional processes and classroom practice (not tested)
Apply a Swiss-cheese layered approach to integrity instead of surveillance (not tested)
Design tasks for cognitive demand, evidence provenance and transparent AI affordances (not tested)
Calibrate AI permission to whether graduates will use AI in their professions; research oral exams, simulations and video scenarios for real-time professions (future research)
limitations: Conceptual, with no empirical evaluation. No limitations section. Several grounding sources are from the school sector or media. Patterns promised in the abstract are not elaborated in the body. Feasibility at scale is asserted, not demonstrated.

quality.note: Full text read. Clear aim; argument cited from literature and policy; conceptual, so no data (q3 N); some abstract claims (ready-to-adopt patterns, feasibility at scale) are not substantiated in the body; no limitations acknowledged.

title: Designing assessments in the generative AI era: A tailored assessment framework for ICT tertiary education
authors: Nadeera Ahangama
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
source_used: Publisher OA PDF (oa_url, link.springer.com); saved as pdfs/R04.pdf; 46 pp. read in full (pp. 1-36 body; appendices skimmed)
ft_reason: HE ICT programmes (AQF 7-9, Australia); assessment redesign for GenAI is the primary focus; peer-reviewed framework paper, 2026, English. Meets IC1-IC5.
study_design: Qualitative interpretivist web-based document analysis with Braun & Clarke six-phase thematic analysis, used to build a conceptual framework (GENESIS) and an Assessment Design Matrix (ADM)
discipline: ICT / computing (cybersecurity, software development, data analytics, information systems, ML)
sample: 80 publicly available English-language web documents (journal articles, university policies/procedures, practice and concept papers, 2023-2025), found by Google searches on 5-9 March 2025; 185 initial codes; saturation reported at 72 documents
genai_tools: GenAI generally (ChatGPT, GPT-4, OpenAI Codex mentioned); the author used ChatGPT (GPT-4o) and Gemini 2.5 Flash for copy-editing only

key_findings.finding: The thematic analysis produced 7 key themes and 70 subthemes. The author argues they form a sequence for institution-wide reform: values, governance, support infrastructure, AI-integrated curriculum, then graduate competencies, strategies and methods.

18 assessment strategies were identified. They include in-person assessment of foundational knowledge, multi-staged connected scaffolding, assessing process over product, personalised authentic contexts, GenAI de-scaffolding, pre-testing tasks with GenAI, and invigilated gatekeeping assessments.

19 assessment methods were listed. Examples are process documentation with iterative evidence, debugging/code-tracing tasks, hackathons, controlled exams, interviews/presentations/demonstrations with Q&A to check authenticity, milestone group projects and multi-stage essays.

Securing every task was described as unrealistic. Instead, programmes should identify key stage-gate assessments (e.g. capstones, demonstrations) for heightened security, and use assessment triangulation across the degree.
Detection tools raised concerns about false positives, bias and fairness, including for non-native English speakers. The sources favour process-oriented, in-person evidence collection over detection.

dimensions.authenticity: Recommends personalised, authentic-context and real-life problem-solving tasks, mapped to ICT graduate competencies (AS9, AM12, AM16; pp. 19-21).
dimensions.capability_verification: Proposes in-person assessment of foundational ICT knowledge and Q&A in interviews and demonstrations to verify depth of understanding (AS1, AM15; pp. 17, 21).
dimensions.integrity_security: Proposes securing selected gatekeeping assessments through supervision/invigilation rather than every task, and moving away from reliance on detection (AC4, AS18, G3; pp. 10, 14, 20).
dimensions.lo_alignment: The ADM links graduate competencies, strategies and methods, and the author maps it to constructive alignment and evidence-centred design (pp. 26-34; Table 3).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Calls for institutions to quantify the AI use allowed for each assessment type and to treat GenAI literacy and prompt engineering as graduate attributes (G2, AC3, GC1, GC8; pp. 9, 14-17).
dimensions.scalability: Claims the ADM can be scaled and adapted to other disciplines by changing graduate attributes, but this has not been empirically tested (p. 36).
dimensions.workload: Notes the need to recalibrate assessment volume as staged and supervised tasks grow, and lists workload pressure as an implementation challenge (AC2, p. 13; p. 36).
dimensions.feasibility: Names staff resistance, resource limits and workload as practical barriers to implementation (p. 36).
dimensions.process_visibility: Recommends process-over-product assessment using prompts, reflective commentaries, planning notes and time-stamped drafts (AS7, AM1; pp. 18, 20).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Highlights equitable access to GenAI tools, detector bias against non-native speakers, and challenges for neurodivergent and socially anxious students with new formats such as in-class Q&A (G5, SI3, SI5; pp. 10-12).

author_recommendations: Adopt the five-pillar GENESIS framework as an institution-wide approach to assessment reform, starting from values and governance (not tested)
Use the Assessment Design Matrix: select at least one graduate competency, strategy and method per assessment and verify the alignment (not tested)
Secure key gatekeeping assessments (e.g. capstones, core technical units) through supervision/invigilation rather than securing every task (not tested)
Pre-test assessment tasks with GenAI before release (not tested)
Empirically validate GENESIS/ADM through pilots, educator/student feedback and longitudinal mixed-methods studies
limitations: Author-stated: the derived lists are limited to what the analysed documents covered; data were limited to public, English-language web documents from a short period, which may not reflect internal practice or tacit knowledge; the frameworks have not been empirically validated (p. 36). Reviewer note: single analyst with no reported second coder; the documents were selected by Google search-result order.

quality.note: Clear RQ; transparent document-analysis/TA procedure with dates, search strings and an 80-document appendix; themes are backed by source excerpts; limitations stated. Caveats: single coder, and the frameworks are unvalidated.

title: Coauthorship integrity: Reconceptualising assessment validity for the age of generative artificial intelligence
authors: Mohsen Ebrahimzadeh; Antonette Shibani; Simon Buckingham Shum
ft_reason: University context (non-proctored writing assessment); assessment validity and academic integrity are the primary focus; GenAI/LLM-based AI Viva; peer-reviewed journal article; 2026, English. Meets IC1-IC5 on full text.
study_design: Conceptual/framework paper (Coauthorship Integrity as a new source of validity evidence) plus proof-of-concept design of an LLM 'AI Viva' prototype and a preliminary expert evaluation (think-aloud, 0-10 ratings and semi-structured interviews)
discipline: Not discipline-specific (writing assessment generally); expert evaluators from linguistics, education, urban studies, futures studies and museology
level: Higher education (general); evaluation used academic staff, not students
sample: 8 expert educators at UTS (3 subject-matter experts, 5 also assessment experts; teaching experience M = 10.5 years, SD = 6.07), each evaluating the prototype on a journal paper they brought (self-authored in 7 of 8 cases); sessions about 90 min (two about 160 min)
genai_tools: GPT-4-1106 via the Microsoft Azure Playground Assistant (university tenant); system prompt of about 29,000 words defining 30 item variants

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that GenAI use in non-proctored writing threatens all five AERA/APA/NCME sources of validity evidence, and propose Coauthorship Integrity (whether the student can account for and defend the ideas in a possibly AI-coauthored text) as an additional, foundational source of validity evidence.

The AI Viva prototype generates comprehension items (multiple-choice, matching, true/false, cloze and open-ended) from the submitter's own text across all six levels of Bloom's revised taxonomy, scores responses, gives a structured feedback report and invites follow-up dialogue.

Experts rated open-ended items higher for checking comprehension (means 8.38-9.00 for Remember to Analyze and Create levels) than recognition items such as multiple-choice (6.38) and cloze (6.25); perceived difficulty rose broadly from Remember to Create.

Scoring accuracy and feedback quality were rated highly for items 1-8 (means about 8.1-9.6), and in post-viva dialogue the agent held its score of 0 for a deliberately irrelevant answer when the expert contested it; Evaluate- and Create-level answers were not scored because of time limits.
The authors position the AI Viva as formative only at this stage; summative use would require assessment-security measures, and preventing AI-on-AI cheating remains unresolved.

dimensions.authenticity: Notes that shifting to proctored exams in response to GenAI shrinks assessment variety and authenticity (Sec 2.5).
dimensions.capability_verification: Proposes verifying students' epistemic ownership of their writing through LLM-generated, text-specific comprehension questions and dialogue (Sec 3-5).
dimensions.integrity_security: Reframes integrity from a provenance problem to a validity problem; acknowledges that summative use would need identity verification and lockdown, and that AI-on-AI cheating is unresolved (Sec 2, Sec 8.3, Sec 8.6).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Items are mapped to Bloom's revised taxonomy levels, but alignment to course learning outcomes is not tested (Sec 5.3).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Accepts human/AI coauthorship as pervasive and locates misconduct in a lack of accountability for the work rather than AI use itself (Sec 1, Sec 9).
dimensions.scalability: Argues AI Vivas could deliver viva-like evidence at scale, unlike labour-intensive human vivas; scale is not demonstrated (Sec 3, Sec 9).
dimensions.workload: Human vivas and interactive orals are described as resource- and time-intensive for large cohorts, motivating automation (Sec 3).
dimensions.feasibility: Preliminary expert evaluation supports technical feasibility, but only with high-quality expert texts and a researcher driving a basic chat interface (Sec 6.2, Sec 8.6).
dimensions.process_visibility: The dialogic mode is presented as a way to elicit response-process evidence about students' reasoning (Sec 8.1.3).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: A text-based rather than spoken viva was chosen partly because verbal formats can disadvantage students with language or accessibility needs (Sec 4).

author_recommendations: Adopt Coauthorship Integrity as an additional source of validity evidence for non-proctored assessment (not tested).
Use AI Vivas formatively to build students' metacognitive awareness of how they use GenAI (preliminary expert evaluation only; not tested with students).
Treat any summative use with great caution and add security measures such as identity verification and locked-down or invigilated conditions (not tested).
Ground the LLM in quality-assured sources to avoid reinforcing misconceptions in the student's text (not tested).
Develop 'AI Viva Analytics' to identify cohort misconceptions under clear privacy governance (not tested).
limitations: Authors acknowledge: small expert sample (n = 8) using high-quality, mostly self-authored texts, which is an optimal case and may inflate performance; no testing with students or student texts; Evaluate/Create items not scored; text-only prototype cannot handle multimodal or mathematical content and does not simulate oral social dynamics; risk of reinforcing misconceptions in the source text; unresolved AI-on-AI cheating for summative use (Sec 8.6). In addition, the qualitative analysis procedure for interviews is not described, and ratings are descriptive only.

quality.note: Re-appraised on full text. Clear aims and RQs; conceptual argument grounded in the AERA et al. (2014) Standards; expert sample and procedure described (Table 1, Sec 6); ratings and dialogue examples support the modest proof-of-concept claims; explicit limitations section. Evidence is preliminary and expert-only, so it does not show effects on students.

title: Assessing students' DRIVE: A framework to evaluate learning through interactions with generative AI
authors: Manuel Oliveira; Carlos Zednik; Gunter J.T. Bombaerts; Bert M. Sadowski; Rianne Conijn
source_used: Authors' preprint on PsyArXiv/OSF (osf.io/cne9j_v4, file 'preprint_2025_oliveira_et_al_Assessing_students_DRIVE.pdf', last updated 16 July 2025; OpenAlex lists it as the accepted version). Saved as pdfs/R17.pdf. ScienceDirect and the TU/e repository PDF returned 403 or a bot challenge to automated access. Page numbers below are the preprint's printed page numbers, which may differ from the published version.
ft_reason: University courses (BSc/MSc); assessment of learning through graded GenAI interaction logs is the primary focus; GenAI; peer-reviewed journal; 2025, English. Meets IC1-IC5.
study_design: Exploratory multi-method study: framework and taxonomy development, plus correlational and descriptive analysis of annotated student-GenAI interaction logs against essay grades
discipline: Philosophy and ethics of AI / data science ethics courses at a STEM university
sample: 445 students enrolled across 3 course offerings (2023-24, 2024-25); 103 opted to use GenAI; 70 essays with logs annotated (1,450 prompts); 4 annotators; inter-rater subset of 33 logs / 772 annotations
genai_tools: ChatGPT (48/70), Claude (1/70), unreported (21/70)

key_findings.finding: Process-focused GenAI interaction scores correlated strongly with traditional essay scores (r = 0.54, 95% CI 0.34-0.68, n = 70; Spearman rho = 0.54). The authors interpret this as initial support for grading interaction logs.

High essay scores were linked to a 'targeted improvement partnership' (text refinement, critical checks, relating concepts). High interaction scores were linked to a 'collaborative intellectual partnership' focused on idea development. Low scores were linked to basic information retrieval or passive task delegation.

The two assessment approaches mostly agreed (21/22 classifications had overlapping CIs). FDR-corrected tests found 5 divergences, with process-focused grading rewarding conceptual and exploratory engagement more than essay grading did.
Inter-rater agreement on the taxonomy was moderate (mean Cohen's kappa 0.44), with some subcategories showing very low agreement.
Teachers noticed fewer students choosing to use GenAI once interaction logs were formally graded. The authors also flag that fabricated logs ('meta-prompting') threaten validity.

dimensions.authenticity: GenAI use was permitted in real graded coursework, and assessment considered how students actually worked with AI (Sec 5.2-5.3, pp. 10-11).
dimensions.capability_verification: Interaction logs were used to make students' domain knowledge and reasoning visible (Visible Expertise), alongside the essay (Sec 3.2, pp. 7-8).
dimensions.integrity_security: Notes that logs could be fabricated to match the rubric ('meta-prompting') and suggests adding student reflections (Sec 10.2, p. 27).
dimensions.lo_alignment: The taxonomy and rubric were derived from course learning outcomes on argumentative and ethical reasoning (Sec 5.4, p. 11; Sec 6, p. 12).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Distinguishes productive interaction profiles (directive, idea-developing, critical) from passive delegation and information retrieval (Sec 9.2.2, pp. 22-23).
dimensions.scalability: Suggests automated classification may eventually help, but says human oversight remains essential (Sec 10.1, p. 26).
dimensions.feasibility: About a third of AI users' logs (33/103) were unusable or excluded because of broken links, messy screenshots or negligible content (Sec 5.2, p. 10; Sec 7, p. 14).
dimensions.process_visibility: Central focus: submitted GenAI interaction logs were graded with a rubric as process evidence (Table 2, p. 13).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: All courses included a lecture on argumentative writing and prompting to reduce disparities in GenAI proficiency (Sec 5.3, p. 11).

author_recommendations: Combine traditional essay assessment with evaluation of interaction logs to capture complementary aspects of learning
Design AI-use rubrics that distinguish interaction patterns according to course learning goals (not tested beyond this study)
Explore student perspectives before introducing process-focused grading of AI use (not tested)
Add student reflections on their AI-assisted process to counter fabricated logs (not tested)
Refine the taxonomy for other disciplines and remove low-agreement items
limitations: Author-stated: mainly philosophy/ethics courses at one university, which limits generalisability; subcategories need adjustment for other disciplines; findings reflect one technological moment; risk of fabricated logs; some taxonomy items had low inter-rater agreement (Sec 10.2, pp. 26-27). Reviewer note: self-selected AI users (23%); correlational design.

quality.note: Clear RQs; appropriate exploratory multi-method design; detailed sample and annotation procedure with reliability; results reported with CIs and FDR correction; limitations explicit. Appraised from the accepted-version preprint.

title: Embracing a new world: authentic assessment designs in an age of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)
authors: Feng Su; Michael O'Dea; Margaret Wood; Eva Seidl
venue: Perspectives: Policy and Practice in Higher Education
source_used: Liverpool Hope University repository (HIRA eprint 4834). The file is the published CC BY-NC-ND article PDF. Saved as pdfs/R23.pdf. The T&F oa_url returned a bot-check page. Page numbers are the journal's printed page numbers.
ft_reason: HE context; authentic assessment design in response to GenAI is the primary focus; GenAI; peer-reviewed (two anonymous reviewers acknowledged); 2026, English.
study_design: Conceptual paper informed by a rapid review (2 journals plus 2 blog platforms), with four illustrative practice scenarios
discipline: Multi-disciplinary: social sciences, translation/interpreting language education, computer science (databases), applied medical sciences
level: Undergraduate (final-year social sciences; second-year CS; second-year medical sciences); language course level not reported
sample: Rapid review: 55 articles screened, 12 included (Assessment & Evaluation in HE, IETI; 2022-2024) plus 14 blog pieces (WonkHE, THE Campus; 2023-2024). Scenario cohorts' n not reported.
genai_tools: ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, DeepSeek (Scenario 1); ChatGPT (Scenarios 3 and 4); unspecified GenAI (Scenario 2)

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that GenAI lets authenticity be reconceived as hybrid and relational, shown through transparent and purposeful student interaction with AI.

The review literature suggests that AI use cannot be reliably detected, that students are unclear about what use is acceptable, and that tutors may need to combine process, content analysis and direct assessment methods instead of detection tools.

In Scenario 3 (second-year CS database module), the brief was run through ChatGPT before release. Its output was critiqued in class, students had to produce work better than it, and marks were reweighted towards process justification, evaluation and reflection. The authors report positive student response and less need for the marker to second-guess plagiarism.

In Scenario 1, students critiqued a 500-word AI response and wrote AI-free reflections, declaring the tool and prompts used. Students valued the clear guidance, but some raised concerns about unequal access to paid AI tools and inaccurate outputs.

The authors conclude that no single solution exists ('silver buckshot'): authentic assessment should be combined with staff and student AI literacy programmes and institution-wide AI assessment frameworks such as the AIAS.

dimensions.authenticity: Core focus: draws on Ashford-Rowe et al.'s critical elements and McArthur's social-value view, and shows authenticity through AI-integrated tasks (pp. 1-2, 6-9).
dimensions.capability_verification: Cites interactive orals and viva elements as a way to support integrity, and Scenario 1 requires AI-free critical reflection (pp. 4, 7).
dimensions.integrity_security: Argues for moving the focus from detection and misconduct towards integrating GenAI, since detection is unreliable (pp. 5-6).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Scenario 3 adjusted marking criteria to reward higher-order thinking and metacognition (p. 8).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Calls for clear, standardised guidance on when and how students may use GenAI, e.g. adopting the AIAS at institutional level (p. 10).
dimensions.workload: Cites Tight (2024): fewer but more meaningful assessments to reduce over-assessment (p. 5).
dimensions.feasibility: Scenario 3 reports that adapting an existing authentic assessment needed only a relatively simple change to the marking criteria (p. 8).
dimensions.process_visibility: Scenarios require prompt/tool declarations and reward descriptions of process and justification of decisions (pp. 7-8).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Raises unequal access to premium AI tools and the potential of GenAI to support students with disabilities such as dyslexia (pp. 4, 6-7).

author_recommendations: Design GenAI into authentic assessment tasks, e.g. critiquing AI outputs or outperforming an AI baseline (illustrated through scenarios, not formally evaluated)
Pre-run assessment briefs through GenAI and reweight criteria towards higher-order thinking and process (not tested)
Develop GenAI literacy for both staff and students (not tested)
Adopt an institution-wide AI assessment framework (e.g. AIAS) for clarity and transparency of AI use (not tested)
Leaders should engage with postplagiarism and generativism ideas when rethinking assessment fundamentals (not tested)
limitations: No explicit limitations section. Reviewer note: the rapid review covered only two journals and two blog platforms; scenario outcomes are anecdotal practitioner reflections with no reported n or systematic data collection.

quality.note: Clear question; conceptual argument grounded in a documented rapid review; but the scenario evidence is anecdotal with unreported samples, and no limitations are acknowledged.

title: Generative AI in computing education: A systematic review and a framework for responsible integration
authors: Arun Kumar; Thakerng Wongsirichot; Aziz Nanthaamornphong
ft_reason: Systematic review of GenAI in computing/programming education, primarily HE; RQ3 on assessment redesign and integrity is a substantial strand (AI-resistant assessment is the densest theme); peer-reviewed journal (CAEAI); 2026; English.
study_design: Systematic literature review (Kitchenham & Charters; Wohlin snowballing from 7 seeds; PRISMA 2020 reporting) with 10-item quality appraisal, thematic synthesis (Cruzes & Dyba) and a derived framework (VIE)
country: Not applicable (review); authors based in India and Thailand; corpus mainly North America, Northern Europe and Australasia
discipline: Computing and programming education
level: Primarily higher education (CS1 30 studies, mixed 34, intermediate 5, advanced 3); limited secondary/vocational coverage
sample: 72 primary studies (2022-2026) from 33 venues, out of 99 candidates; mean QA 8.32/10; 61 full-weight studies
genai_tools: ChatGPT/GPT-3.5/GPT-4 (33 studies), GitHub Copilot (12), Codex (9), multiple tools (30)

key_findings.finding: Thirteen studies show most standard programming assessments can be completed by current GenAI. Visual-spatial tasks and under-specified problems are partial exceptions, and one study found authentic context-specific tasks had 41% AI completion versus 82% for standard exam tasks.

AI-resistant assessment design is the most densely evidenced theme (26 studies). Strategies include process-visible work (staged portfolios, code journals), oral defence/viva and live coding (endorsed by 12 studies), authentic contextualised tasks, Prompt Problems and perturbation.
Self-reported undisclosed AI use on assessments is commonly 45-65% (13 studies). Policy ambiguity predicts it, and peer norms were the strongest predictor of misconduct intention in one SEM study.

AI detection is thinly evidenced (3 studies). The best result reported was 89% accuracy with an 8% false-positive rate. The authors argue false positives fall unevenly on students such as non-native speakers and that accuracy decays across model generations.

The VIE framework (Verification, Implementation, Equity) requires graded, observable critical engagement with AI output, institutional capacity (policy, faculty development, assessment redesign) and equity-aware design. Each is treated as interdependent.

dimensions.authenticity: Authentic, context-specific tasks needing local knowledge are among the most AI-resistant strategies; one primary study showed roughly half the AI completion rate of standard tasks (Sec 4.4.1, Sec 4.4.5).
dimensions.capability_verification: Finds submitted code no longer reliably shows skill; oral defence and live coding are the most AI-resistant in practice because they require real-time independent reasoning (Sec 1, Sec 4.4.5).
dimensions.integrity_security: Synthesises assessment vulnerability, misconduct prevalence (45-65%), weak detection and policy landscape; argues redesign and norm-shifting outperform detection-centric enforcement (Sec 4.4).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Argues GenAI fuses tool use, learning and assessment in computing, so artefact-based assessment cannot separate learning from delegation (Sec 1).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Recommends graduated, competence-gated AI access and explicit AI literacy; notes a contested minority view favouring fully AI-permitted assessment (Sec 4.4.5, Sec 4.5.1, Sec 4.5.2).
dimensions.workload: Fig. 7 positions strategies by implementation effort; code-explanation components are a lower-effort entry point than oral defence; AI-assisted grading reported to reduce instructor workload (Sec 4.4.5, Fig. 7).
dimensions.feasibility: Faculty workshops produced oral-defence and portfolio templates rated implementable within one semester; faculty development is a documented gap (Sec 4.5.4, Sec 5.4).
dimensions.process_visibility: Process-visible assessments (staged portfolios, code journals, think-aloud) and IDE/prompt-log analytics are proposed to make verification observable, subject to privacy and consent (Sec 4.4.5, Sec 5.5).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Equity is a co-equal VIE requirement covering skill-gap and resource-gap mechanisms; detector false positives may disproportionately affect non-native speakers (Sec 4.4.3, Sec 5.1).

author_recommendations: Redesign at least one high-stakes assessment per course to include an oral component or process-visible element (not tested by the review)
Introduce GenAI gradually after foundational competence, with course-level differentiated access policies (not tested by the review)
Teach AI literacy explicitly, including prompt engineering and AI error analysis (not tested by the review)
Prefer assessment redesign and norm-shifting (honour codes, pledges, modelled disclosure) over detection-centric enforcement (not tested)
Invest in tiered, role-aware faculty development and equity-of-access policies; address seven research gaps such as longitudinal and cross-national studies (not tested)
limitations: Snowballing from 7 seeds may miss papers outside citation chains; English-only; screening and QA by a single rater (second coder for thematic coding only on 18 studies, kappa 0.62); QA for some papers without full text was based on venue and extraction data; Table 4 counts flagged as needing re-tally after the supplementary search; constructs are heterogeneously operationalised; corpus skewed to English-speaking, well-resourced contexts.

quality.note: Explicit RQs, protocol, PRISMA flow, QA instrument, IRR and replication package; corpus well described (Tables 2-4). Threats to validity discussed in depth. Minor concerns: single-rater screening/QA and an internally inconsistent Table 4 note.

title: Using Generative AI to Promote Psychological, Feedback, and Artificial Intelligence Literacies in Undergraduate Psychology
authors: Jenny L. Richmond; Kate Nicholls
ft_reason: Full text confirms undergraduate psychology (HE) assessment redesign integrating ChatGPT, evaluated with cohort data; peer-reviewed journal (Teaching of Psychology; online 2024, issue 2025); English. Non-computing but meets IC1-IC5.
study_design: Teaching-practice evaluation: description of a three-phase assessment redesign; analysis of students' rubric grades of ChatGPT output (chi-square) and comparison of grades with the previous peer-review cohort (t-tests); non-randomised historical comparison
discipline: Psychology (second-year Social and Developmental Psychology)
sample: n = 363 undergraduates (Term 1 2023; opt-out consent, none opted out); comparison cohort Term 1 2022 gradebook data, N = 397 (waiver of consent)
genai_tools: ChatGPT (or another GenAI tool)

key_findings.finding: Phase 1 of the three-phase Media Assignment was redesigned: students had ChatGPT draft a media release, graded it against the script-revision rubric and listed three strengths, weaknesses and revision priorities (10%); Phase 2 revised it with tracked changes (20%); the Phase 3 final video (30%) was unchanged.

Students rated ChatGPT's draft highly for Style (92% above Pass) but poorly for Aims/Methods/Results (94% Credit or lower); the association between criterion and grade was large (chi-square(4) = 317.48, p < .001, adjusted Cramer's V = 0.66).

Students performed well on the AI critique task (mean 72.7; 44% Distinction or High Distinction), though a few gave ChatGPT high grades for Aims/Methods/Results, suggesting some need more scaffolding to check accuracy.
Script revision grades were higher than in the 2022 peer-review cohort (69.4 vs 66.7; t(733.05) = 4.93, p < .001, d = 0.36), but final video grades did not differ (71.2 vs 70.3; p = .129).

The authors are cautious: gains may reflect early rubric engagement or simply revising stylistically strong AI text. They note revising draws on different competencies from writing, and argue assessment should evidence the learning process rather than the artefact.

dimensions.authenticity: Science-communication task for a lay audience, with multi-source feedback, emulating professional writing (Introduction).
dimensions.integrity_security: The original task was judged at risk because ChatGPT is good at summarising and style; the redesign makes AI use mandatory and visible rather than prohibited (Introduction).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Students applied the actual marking rubric to AI output early, aligning critique with the criteria for later phases (Table 1; Discussion).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: GenAI use was required for the first draft and scaffolded through critique and tracked-change revision (Introduction; Table 1).
dimensions.scalability: Implemented in a large course (n = 363) with tutorial instructors marking (Method).
dimensions.feasibility: Replaced the peer-review step with an AI-critique step within an existing three-phase assessment; materials shared on OSF (Table 1).
dimensions.process_visibility: Tracked changes on the AI draft and an optional rejoinder document how students revised; authors call for LMS version control to document process (Table 1; Discussion).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: ChatGPT drafts of consistent quality made the review step more equitable than reviewing peers' variable drafts (Discussion).

author_recommendations: Have students critique a GenAI draft against the marking rubric early in a staged assessment (evaluated in this course)
Provide more scaffolding for verifying the accuracy of GenAI output (not tested)
Consider having students reflect on the AI draft and then write their own draft rather than revise the AI text (planned for next implementation; not tested)
Shift assessment toward the learning process, with LMS tools for version control and process documentation (not tested)
limitations: Non-randomised comparison with the previous cohort; the authors cannot rule out that gains came from revising stylistically good AI text rather than rubric engagement. Only two of six rubric criteria are reported. No demographic data (sex and age estimated from school norms). Single course and institution.

quality.note: Full text read. Clear aims and hypotheses; appropriate descriptive and inferential analysis for a teaching evaluation; sample and data collection described with ethics; claims cautious; the key limitation (confounded cohort comparison) is acknowledged in the Discussion.

title: Comparison of generative AI performance on undergraduate and postgraduate written assessments in the biomedical sciences
authors: Andrew Evan Williams
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
source_used: Publisher OA PDF (oa_url, link.springer.com); saved as pdfs/R53.pdf; 22 pp. read in full
ft_reason: UK HE (FHEQ levels 4-7); tests how vulnerable written essay assessments are to GenAI and what that means for assessment validity and integrity, which is a substantial focus; GenAI; peer-reviewed; 2024, English.
study_design: Evaluation study: GenAI-generated essays marked blind by four independent markers against FHEQ-mapped criteria, with inter-rater reliability (Kendall's W)
discipline: Biomedical sciences
sample: 4 essay questions (one per FHEQ level, UCL courses) x 3 GenAI tools = 12 AI essays, each marked by 4 independent markers; prompts submitted 11 Aug - 9 Sep 2023
genai_tools: ChatGPT 3.5 (free), Google Bard, Microsoft Bing (GPT-4 based)

key_findings.finding: ChatGPT scored highest at every level: total about 70.7% (L4), 70.4% (L5), 71.85% (L6) and 69.75% (L7), i.e. high or borderline-first-class attainment. Bard was next and Bing lowest.

No tool supplied appropriate scientific references. Bing produced fully fabricated, realistically formatted references, and Bard misreported its word count.

Marker agreement was high for the undergraduate essays (e.g. total-score W = 0.708-0.877) but lower for level 7 (W = 0.464).

dimensions.integrity_security: The author frames the findings as having implications for the design, implementation and grading of written assessments and for academic integrity (abstract; Conclusion p. 20).
dimensions.lo_alignment: AI output was benchmarked against FHEQ level descriptors and marking criteria mapped to them (pp. 4-5; Table 1).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Recommends training students on the strengths and limits of LLMs, in the context of institutional integrity policies (pp. 19-20).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Tools were chosen on the basis of free student access (p. 3).

author_recommendations: Train students in appropriate use of generative AI and its limitations, within institutional academic integrity policies (not tested)
Teachers may supervise or guide students' use of GenAI tools to ensure accuracy (not tested)
Future research should compare AI and student scripts blind, cover other assessment types (short answer, MCQ), and examine AI in assessment design and grading
limitations: Author-stated: compared AI tools only, with no comparison with student-written scripts at equivalent levels; only essays were tested, not other assessment types (p. 20). Reviewer note: one question per level and single-prompt generation with 2023 tool versions; LLMs have since changed.

quality.note: Clear aim; blinded multi-marker design with reliability statistics suits the question; materials and prompts fully described; results tabulated; limitations stated. Small item sample (4 questions).

title: Assessment Reform for the Age of Artificial Intelligence
authors: Jason M. Lodge; Sarah Howard; Margaret Bearman; Phillip Dawson
venue: TEQSA (Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency)
source_used: TEQSA PDF (oa_url, teqsa.gov.au); saved as pdfs/R68.pdf; 12 pp. read in full (document dated November 2023). Page numbers are the document's printed page numbers.
ft_reason: Australian HE; assessment reform for GenAI is the primary focus; AI; formal expert-consensus framework (principles and propositions) commissioned by the national regulator (IC4 via the formal-framework route, not peer reviewed); 2023, English.
study_design: Expert-consensus guidance/framework: two guiding principles and five propositions developed at a two-day TEQSA/UTS expert forum (August 2023), then wider expert consultation and public consultation
discipline: Cross-disciplinary (examples include commerce, physiotherapy, arts, science, law, journalism, interior design, computer science)
sample: Not applicable (expert forum of named contributors plus a wider consultation group and public consultation; no empirical data)
genai_tools: Generative AI generally (large language models); no specific tools

key_findings.finding: The document states that non-invigilated tasks are hard to design so that they preclude substantial GenAI use, and that reliable detection appears almost impossible. Blanket bans are described as oversimplified.
Guiding principle 2: trustworthy judgements need multiple, inclusive, contextualised assessments, triangulated, because no single assessment type can handle all desirable and undesirable AI use.

There are five propositions: appropriate, authentic engagement with AI; a systemic, program-level approach; assessing the process of learning; appropriate collaboration with peers and AI; and security at meaningful points across a program.

Proposition 5 recommends securing key program-level assessment moments rather than every task, because security is resource-intensive. One example is a computer science capstone secured through interactive code reviews, resourced by removing a first-year exam.
The authors acknowledge that workload and accreditation issues will be barriers, and that staff capability building will be needed.

dimensions.authenticity: Proposition 1 calls for appropriate, authentic engagement with AI aligned with disciplinary or professional values (p. 3).
dimensions.capability_verification: Proposition 5 calls for evidencing what students can do without AI at key progression and completion points (p. 6).
dimensions.integrity_security: Argues for targeted security at meaningful points across a program rather than securing every task (p. 6).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Proposition 2 calls for program-level assessment design aligned with program learning outcomes and qualifications (p. 4).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: States that trustworthy assessment requires telling students clearly what is and is not permissible when working with AI (p. 5).
dimensions.scalability: Program-level securing is presented as a response to the infeasibility of applying resource-intensive security to all tasks (p. 6).
dimensions.workload: Acknowledges workload as a barrier to reform at scale (p. 7).
dimensions.feasibility: Acknowledges accreditation barriers and the need to build staff capability (p. 7).
dimensions.process_visibility: Proposition 3 calls for evidencing the learning process over time, e.g. decision trails, logs or diaries of collaboration with AI (pp. 4-5).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Grounds the reform in fairness, accessibility, equity and inclusion, and says access to and capability with AI should not be assumed (pp. 2, 5).

author_recommendations: Design assessment for appropriate, authentic engagement with AI, taught explicitly across a program (not tested)
Take a systemic, program-level approach to assessment (not tested)
Assess the process of learning, including students' judgement in using AI (not tested)
Articulate permissible ways of working with peers and AI, e.g. requiring explanation of prompts used (not tested)
Secure key program-level assessment moments (e.g. capstones via interactive code reviews or targeted exams) rather than every task (not tested)
limitations: Author-stated: not prescriptive or formulaic; intended to be revisited as technology evolves; workload and accreditation barriers acknowledged (pp. 1, 6-7). Reviewer note: expert opinion with few cited references (3); not peer reviewed; no empirical evaluation.

quality.note: Clear purpose; consensus process described (forum, consultation); but the propositions rest on expert judgement with minimal cited evidence and are not empirically supported; limitations and barriers acknowledged.

title: AI-Assisted Assessment: A Dual Perspective on Effective Usage Plans for Students and Teachers
authors: José Manuel Martins Ferreira
ft_reason: Amendment 3 (redesign focus): AI-assisted grading with NotebookLM
study_design: Single-course pedagogical experiment/case study: NotebookLM grade recommendations for 8 group reports (two runs) compared with teacher grades; student experience and satisfaction questionnaire
discipline: Computer Science (Hardware/Software Codesign)
sample: 30 students in 8 groups of 3-4 (2024/25 edition); 19 questionnaire responses (63%)
genai_tools: Google NotebookLM (grading support and podcasts); students used ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Claude and others under a course AI usage plan

key_findings.finding: The course combines a 3-week group project (10-page IEEE-format report plus source files, with a section or annex on how AI was used; 50%) and a final written exam (50%), under an AI usage plan given to students before the course.

NotebookLM was given only each group's PDF report and a class-approved common prompt grading seven aspects (four implementations, language, template compliance, AI-use description); it assisted the teacher, who had graded first, rather than grading itself.
Two runs a week apart gave identical partial grades in 40 of 56 cases (71.4%), with a 2-point difference in only 2 cases (3.6%).

AI-proposed and teacher grades differed in both directions, normally by less than 10% but by more than 30% in 3 cases; the author attributes gaps to NotebookLM lacking access to figures, source files and annexes (e.g., one group's AI use was documented only in an annex).

Students were initially reluctant ('AI grading AI'); 63.2% gave the top two scores to the grading method but only 42.1% to NotebookLM's assessments (26.3% gave the lowest), and 68.4% accepted AI-assisted grading (5 of 19 preferred teacher-only).

dimensions.integrity_security: Anonymous submission via Wiseflow; NotebookLM was considered acceptable for privacy because uploads are not used for training (Sec III.A; Sec III.D).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: A staged AI usage plan guided student AI use; students had to describe their AI use, which was itself graded (Sec II; Table I; Sec III.D).
dimensions.workload: AI-assisted grading is presented as easing a task teachers dislike, giving detailed justifications that may exceed a teacher's (Sec III.C; Sec V).

dimensions.process_visibility: Students were asked to document AI use in the report or an annex (Sec III.D).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: In the earlier course edition, a university-paid OpenAI Plus subscription gave all students equal access (Sec II).

author_recommendations: Use AI as a grading assistant with humans in the loop; avoid unsupervised AI grading (based on this experiment)
Inform students when and how AI is used in grading and involve them in prompt design and procedures (implemented in this course)
Expect grading to involve more face-to-face discussion as students use AI for their work (not tested)
Research how student writing style affects AI-recommended grades (future work)
limitations: Single course, 8 group submissions, 19 survey responses; descriptive results only, with no agreement statistics beyond exact-match counts; the AI had incomplete inputs (no annexes, figures or code), so its accuracy cannot be properly judged; the author is both the teacher-grader and the evaluator; the conclusion that AI-assisted grading 'can be relied upon' goes beyond the data. quality.note: Full text read. Clear aim and sample; small descriptive design; reliance claims are stronger than the AI-teacher discrepancies in Table II support; the tool's input limits are discussed but study limitations are not.

title: Beyond the Code: Evaluating Alternative Assessment Strategies for Integrity and Authentic Learning in AI-Influenced Programming Tasks
