venue: 2026 4th UK-China Teaching, Learning, and Educational Technology (TILE-TEC)
ft_reason: Undergraduate programming module (HE); redesign of programming assessment for integrity and validity under GenAI (viva, live demo, repository history); IEEE TILE-TEC conference; 2026; English.
study_design: Two-phase practitioner action research (baseline take-home plus viva and live demo; then the redesigned TAP framework) with descriptive comparison of assessment scores, a composite Learning Integrity Score and a student perception questionnaire
country: Not reported (authors at University of Stirling, UK, and a partner college in Chengdu, China; study site not stated)
discipline: Computing (programming-focused module)
sample: 60 undergraduates in one programming module taught by the researcher (convenience sample); assessment data anonymised
genai_tools: Generative AI / LLM coding tools in general (none named); AI use not prohibited

key_findings.finding: In Phase 1, take-home scores averaged about 83.8% but viva scores averaged about 35.2% and live code demonstration about 43.9%. Students with high take-home marks often could not explain or reproduce their own code.
A Learning Integrity Score (LIS) measured agreement between the submission and supervised performance. In Phase 1, 45% of students had an LIS of zero and only 10% scored above 50.

After the TAP redesign (repository with version history, structured viva, supervised live demo), averages were about 63% (repository), 56% (viva) and 58% (demo). Mean LIS rose from about 11.7 to about 45.3.
Of the students, 91.7% agreed or strongly agreed that the revised assessment improved learning, 86.7% rated it fair or very fair, and 83.3% preferred it to the traditional take-home model.
Viva performance can reflect anxiety, hesitation or language proficiency. TAP therefore triangulates three kinds of evidence instead of using the viva alone as a proxy for integrity.
key_findings.location: Sec II, Sec III, Sec IV.E

dimensions.authenticity: Framed as moving to authentic, process-oriented evidence of learning rather than product-only grading (Sec I, Sec V).
dimensions.capability_verification: Viva and live demonstration revealed large gaps between submitted code and the ability to explain or reproduce it; triangulation narrowed the gap (Sec IV.A-C).
dimensions.integrity_security: LIS used as an indicator of authorship/integrity; mean LIS rose from about 11.7 to 45.3 after redesign (Sec IV.C).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Grounded in constructive alignment: programming outcomes include explaining logic, justifying design and adapting code, not only correct output (Sec I).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: AI use was not banned; students instead had to demonstrate understanding, ownership and process alongside the product (Sec II, Sec IV.C).
dimensions.feasibility: Implemented within normal module delivery for a 60-student cohort (Sec II).
dimensions.process_visibility: Repository submission with commit and revision history captures incremental development as process evidence (Sec II, Sec III).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Acknowledges oral formats may disadvantage anxious students or those with lower language proficiency; triangulation is intended to be fairer and more inclusive; 86.7% rated it fair (Sec II, Sec IV.D).

author_recommendations: Replace product-only take-home programming assessment with the triangulated TAP model: repository history, structured viva and supervised live demo (tested in one cohort)
Do not treat any single mode, especially the viva, as decisive evidence of integrity (design principle)
Move programming assessment toward process-oriented, multi-modal evidence of capability (general recommendation)
limitations: Single cohort and module, convenience sample, practitioner-researcher; no control group. Phases are confounded (different task formats and weights; Phase 1 already included viva and demo). Descriptive statistics only. LIS is an ad hoc formula. Questionnaire not described. GenAI use was not measured directly. Workload and scalability were not reported, and no explicit study limitations section.

quality.note: Clear aim and suitable action-research design. Context is thin (country, course level, AI use and questionnaire not described). Claims of improved validity rest on descriptive comparisons of non-equivalent phases using an ad hoc index. Limitations of oral formats are discussed.

title: Assessment in the age of artificial intelligence
authors: Zachari Swiecki; Hassan Khosravi; Guanliang Chen; Roberto Martínez‐Maldonado; Jason M. Lodge; Sandra Milligan; Neil Selwyn; Dragan Gašević
ft_reason: Amendment 3 (redesign focus): Pre-GenAI review of AI-enabled assessment systems
study_design: Conceptual/critical narrative review (explicitly non-exhaustive, footnote 2)
country: Australia (author affiliations: Monash, Queensland, Melbourne); setting not country-specific
discipline: General education (not discipline-specific)
level: Education generally (schools and universities); not HE-specific
sample: Not applicable (conceptual review)
genai_tools: AI in assessment broadly: automated question generation, AI-assisted peer assessment, automated essay scoring, Turnitin, electronic assessment platforms, stealth assessment, knowledge tracing, adaptive testing, virtual internships; AI writing tools (Word/Docs suggestions, Grammarly, Sudowrite)

key_findings.finding: The standard assessment paradigm is characterised as onerous, discrete, uniform, inauthentic and antiquated (assessing skills humans now offload to computers).

AI approaches are reviewed under five shifts: onerous to feasible (question generation, AI-assisted peer assessment, writing analytics), discrete to continuous (e-assessment logs, stealth assessment, knowledge tracing, process analytics), uniform to adaptive (computerised adaptive testing), inauthentic to authentic (AI-supported simulations such as virtual internships), and antiquated to modern (AI writing tools).

Six challenges of AI-enabled assessment are raised: sidelining of teacher expertise, black-boxing of accountability, restricting assessment's pedagogical role, assessing limited forms of learning (including possible cultural and ableist bias), surveillance pedagogy, and distributed human-AI assessment models.

Under evidence-centred design, AI implies assessing traits that require human contribution, allowing AI tools during tasks, and accounting for joint human-AI evidence (separating or jointly modelling contributions); prior work has focused mainly on the evidence model.
The authors conclude AI only partially addresses traditional assessment problems and is not a panacea; it brings new challenges for assessment design and implementation.

dimensions.authenticity: Argues traditional tasks are inauthentic (e.g., writing in isolation without tools) and reviews AI-supported simulations such as virtual internships as routes to authentic assessment (Sec 2.1, 3.4).
dimensions.capability_verification: Under human-AI teamwork the evidence model must separate or account for human versus AI contributions to assessment evidence (Sec 4.6).
dimensions.integrity_security: Discusses plagiarism detection (Turnitin) and exam log data for misconduct investigation, and warns that continuous AI monitoring creates surveillance that can erode trust (Sec 3.1.3, 3.2.1, 4.5).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Argues the student model should shift to skills requiring human contribution rather than those AI can do alone (Sec 4.6).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Suggests the task model should allow students to use AI tools during assessment, as professionals do (Sec 3.5, 4.6).
dimensions.scalability: AI-assisted peer assessment and automated scoring are presented as scaling to large classes and MOOCs (Sec 3.1.2-3.1.3).
dimensions.workload: AI can offload task generation, peer-grade aggregation and scoring from educators, but the paper warns of over-reliance on machine outputs (Sec 3.1, 4.1).
dimensions.feasibility: Automated question generation depends on large relevant datasets, and its metrics do not guarantee pedagogical value (Sec 3.1.1).
dimensions.process_visibility: Reviews AI-enabled assessment of learning processes (log, clickstream, multimodal data) rather than only final artefacts (Sec 3.2.4).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Notes uniform assessments may give unequal opportunity, and AI-enabled assessment may encode Western, ableist or neurotypical norms (Sec 2.1, 4.4).

author_recommendations: Design AI-enabled assessment systems whose decisions are explainable to teachers, keeping teachers' judgement in the loop (not tested)
Establish rigorous oversight and clear lines of accountability for AI-produced assessment decisions and how they become grades (not tested)
Shift continuous monitoring toward developmental feedback rather than judgement (not tested)
Extend assessment design theory to the student and task models under human-AI teamwork, not only the evidence model (not tested)
limitations: Authors state the review is not exhaustive and highlights exemplar approaches (footnote 2). Pre-ChatGPT (2022), so it does not address current LLM capabilities. Not HE-specific. No systematic search or appraisal of included studies.

quality.note: Full text read. Clear aim; argument well grounded in cited literature; conceptual, so no data (q3 N). Scope limitation noted only in a footnote and there is no limitations section (q5 Unclear).

title: How university students work on assessment tasks with generative artificial intelligence: matters of judgement
authors: Jack Walton; Margaret Bearman; Nicole Crawford; Joanna Tai; David J. Boud
source_used: Publisher OA full-text HTML at tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02602938.2025.2570328, read in browser (curl PDF returned 403; figshare copy did not download; UTS OPUS copy requires login). No PDF saved. Locations are given by section heading because the HTML has no page numbers (print pages 1066-1082).
ft_reason: HE (Australian undergraduates); focuses on how students use GenAI on assessment tasks, with implications for assessment design and validity; peer reviewed; 2025.
study_design: Qualitative multimodal interview study ('scroll-back' interviews) with holistic narrative analysis
discipline: Multiple (Psychology, Arts, Education, Nursing, Optometry, Biomedical Science, Law, Business, Sociology, Computer Science)
sample: 26 undergraduate interviews at one large Australian university (11 recruited via the disability/accessibility unit, 15 via subject LMS adverts); students self-identified as motivated GenAI users; 30 of 52 judgement events related to assessment were analysed
genai_tools: ChatGPT mainly; GenAI tools in general

key_findings.finding: Identified six categories of student judgement events, from judging knowledge with GenAI through to submitting GenAI content with no judgement at all.
Some students said they had substantially edited GenAI outputs, but their shared traces showed little change. The authors read this as a genuine misjudgement of their own contribution.
key_findings.location: Sec Findings - Misjudging GenAI contributions as their own

key_findings.finding: In open-book online quizzes, some students pasted questions into GenAI and submitted the answers, justifying this as what everyone does. One student called it probably cheating.
key_findings.location: Sec Findings - Submitting GenAI work in the assignment without judging it

key_findings.finding: Authors argue that tasks which can be completed with GenAI in ways that bypass intended learning effectively incentivise copy-paste, so this is a validity and design problem rather than only a cheating problem.
Students' own accounts of what they learned or how they used GenAI did not tell apart students who were becoming less reliant from those who were not.

dimensions.capability_verification: Students' self-reports of their contribution did not match their artefacts, which undermines inferences about what they can do.
dimensions.integrity_security: Shows unsupervised online quizzes being completed by pasting into GenAI, with students rationalising it as normal.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Argues assessments that let GenAI bypass intended learning are invalid in the Dawson et al. sense and incentivise misuse.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Students' judgements about appropriate use were often made without clear guidance and were tangled up with judgements about their own deficits.
dimensions.process_visibility: Recommends interim steps and asking students to evaluate their own contribution, to make the process visible.
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Students with disabilities used GenAI to manage capability gaps and anxiety, which creates learning trade-offs.

author_recommendations: Treat the GenAI challenge as a learning and validity problem rather than mainly a cheating problem (not tested).
Avoid task designs, such as unsupervised online quizzes, that GenAI can complete in ways that bypass intended learning (not tested).
Design assessments that build evaluative judgement about students' own contributions, for example through interim submission steps (not tested).
Explicitly teach and design tasks that integrate 'what is' and 'how to' knowledge (not tested).
limitations: No dedicated limitations section. The authors describe the analysis as highly interpretive and report team disagreement on some interpretations. The sample is one university and self-selected motivated GenAI users, and some participants brought no historical traces.

quality.note: Clear RQs and appropriate qualitative design; recruitment, sample and data collection well described; findings supported by participant quotes and traces. Limitations are not set out explicitly, only touched on in the reflexive comments.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Tertiary Education: Assessment Redesign Principles and Considerations
authors: Che Yee Lye; Lyndon Lim
source_used: Publisher OA full-text HTML at mdpi.com/2227-7102/14/6/569, read in browser (PDF via curl returned 403). No PDF saved. Locations are given by section number.
ft_reason: Tertiary education; assessment redesign and integrity are the primary focus; GenAI; peer-reviewed conceptual/framework paper (AAA principle); 2024.
study_design: Conceptual paper proposing a framework (Against, Avoid and Adopt principle)
discipline: General tertiary education
sample: not applicable (conceptual)
genai_tools: ChatGPT and generative AI in general

key_findings.finding: Proposes the AAA principle, which sorts assessments into Against (no GenAI), Avoid (tasks GenAI does not yet handle well) and Adopt (GenAI integrated at two levels).
Against suits lower-order or certification-required skills, assessed in invigilated GenAI-free exams or supervised in-class formats such as ad hoc Q&A, debates and vivas.
Avoid tasks include higher-order skills, live performance, portfolios and personal reflection or self/peer assessment, contextualised to real-world and personal experience.
Adopt requires students to cite GenAI use, give their prompts and show the outputs. It runs from ideation-only use up to tasks that require critique and refinement of AI output.
Argues detectors are not a tenable solution and an arms race or policing will not fix underlying assessment issues. High assessment load is identified as a driver of misconduct.

dimensions.authenticity: Argues GenAI-integrated tasks are reasonable where graduates will use GenAI at work, and that Avoid tasks should draw on real-world scenarios.
dimensions.capability_verification: Assigns invigilated exams, vivas and live Q&A to skills that must be verified for certification.
dimensions.integrity_security: Frames assessment redesign around academic integrity and rejects detectors as unreliable and harmful to trust.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Uses Archer's assessment purpose triangle to argue that outcomes and assessments should be rethought for fitness for purpose.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Defines two levels of permitted use in Adopt, with citation of use, prompts and outputs.
dimensions.workload: Links high student assessment load to surface learning and misconduct.
dimensions.process_visibility: Adopt requires students to show prompts and outputs and to reflect on their interactions with GenAI.
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Notes digital-divide and fairness concerns about rewarding skilled GenAI users.

author_recommendations: Apply the AAA principle to sort assessments into Against, Avoid or Adopt according to purpose (not tested).
Keep invigilated, GenAI-free conditions for lower-order skills needed for certification (not tested).
Contextualise Avoid tasks to personal experience and human interaction (not tested).
Require citation of GenAI use, prompts and outputs in Adopt tasks (not tested).
Educators should become familiar with GenAI tools faster than students so they can define acceptable uses (not tested).
limitations: Not reported. The paper has no limitations section, and the framework is not empirically evaluated.

quality.note: Conceptual paper with a clear aim, grounded in cited literature (TPB, Archer's assessment purpose triangle, Moorhouse et al.). No data, so q3 = N. The framework is argued but not validated, and limitations are not acknowledged.

title: Changing EAP assessment practices in the age of generative artificial intelligence: The case of Scottish higher education institutions
authors: Lewis Urquhart; Xuan Minh Ngo
venue: Journal of English for Academic Purposes
source_used: Version of record PDF (CC BY) from the University of St Andrews repository (hdl 10023/33407), saved as pdfs/R24.pdf. The ScienceDirect route was blocked by CAPTCHA. Issue date 2026, vol 79; available online Nov 2025.
ft_reason: HE (Scottish universities' EAP provision); assessment change in response to GenAI is the primary focus; peer reviewed; 2025/2026.
study_design: Qualitative case study; semi-structured interviews; thematic analysis
discipline: English for Academic Purposes (pre-sessional and in-sessional/integrated)
sample: 6 EAP academics in leadership roles at 5 Scottish universities, interviewed mid-2024; purposive sampling; institutional websites used to triangulate
genai_tools: ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot (GenAI in general)

key_findings.finding: The five departments made few changes to core task types. Adaptations were mostly to task requirements (GenAI declarations, context-specific prompts such as local case studies, next-day follow-up Q&A after presentations) and to grading.

Grading changes included more weight on contextual relevance than linguistic accuracy, and a switch from anonymised to named marking by course tutors. The tutor-marker change was well received and reportedly coincided with fewer misconduct cases.
Three participants judged GenAI use declarations ineffective. One saw them mainly as an institutional safeguard for imposing penalties, not a deterrent.

Participants mostly favoured authentic and innovative tasks (portfolios with a viva element, reflections, multimodal work, evaluating GenAI output) over a return to exams, but raised workload concerns about marking multiple drafts and doubts that portfolios resist GenAI.

The authors argue that unchanged essays, reports and presentations put the validity of inferences about independent language ability at risk. They attribute slow change to time, approval bureaucracy and staffing pressures.

dimensions.authenticity: Practitioners rejected pen-and-paper exams as inauthentic and favoured authentic, innovative and multimodal tasks.
dimensions.capability_verification: Follow-up Q&A after presentations and spontaneous speaking tasks were used to verify mastery of content.
dimensions.integrity_security: Declarations were seen as ineffective; named marking by tutors who know the students was seen as more effective.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Concern that GenAI integration may require skills beyond EAP outcomes, and that unchanged tasks threaten valid inferences about language ability.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Divided views on integrating GenAI; evaluating GenAI output was being trialled in some programmes.
dimensions.workload: Marking multiple drafts and redesigning assessments were constrained by time, hiring freezes and course-approval processes.
dimensions.feasibility: Institutional bureaucracy and the need for academic board approval slowed changes to task types.
dimensions.process_visibility: Process-oriented elements (drafts, portfolios, follow-up Q&A) were emerging only as incremental adjustments.

author_recommendations: Institutions should support small-scale pilots of innovative or GenAI-integrated assessment (not tested).
Allocate redesign time, streamline assessment amendment approvals, and provide professional development on designing and validating GenAI-resilient assessments (not tested).
Run ongoing professional dialogue and bottom-up development drawing on EAP practitioners' expertise (not tested).
Adopt iterative, locally divergent redesign rather than one-size-fits-all solutions (not tested).
limitations: Small sample (6 participants, 5 institutions, two from one university) at one point in mid-2024, so findings may not generalise. Relies on interview recall, with partial triangulation from websites; some contextual data (student numbers) could not be verified.

quality.note: Clear RQs; appropriate qualitative case design with member checking, an audit trail and researcher triangulation; sample and context described (Tables 1-2); themes supported by quotes; limitations stated (p. 9). The sample is very small.

title: Integrating Generative AI into Programming Education: Student Perceptions and the Challenge of Correcting AI Errors
authors: Dan Kohen-Vacs; Maya Usher; Marc Jansen
venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
source_used: Springer OA PDF (CC BY) from oa_url, saved as pdfs/R33.pdf. Page numbers are journal pages 3166-3184.
ft_reason: HE programming courses; Study 2 evaluates exam tasks built from LLM-generated flawed code (assessment design/validity); GenAI; peer reviewed; 2025.
study_design: Two quantitative studies: cross-sectional survey (Study 1); comparison of exam task scores with paired t-tests (Study 2)
discipline: Computer science / programming (Operations Research and Cryptography courses in Study 2)
sample: Study 1: 64 undergraduates in Israel (online questionnaire, March 2024; 83% female). Study 2: 147 undergraduates in Germany, exam scores from 6 exams over 3 terms (Winter 2022/23 to Winter 2023/24; 81% male)
genai_tools: LLMs in general (ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot named); exam code produced by an LLM (model not specified)

key_findings.finding: In Summer 2023 and Winter 2023/24, students scored significantly lower on exam tasks that required correcting LLM-generated flawed Java code than on instructor-designed tasks, in both courses.
In Winter 2022/23 there was no significant difference, but overall performance was low that term (pass rates 20% and 29.41%), which the authors say may have masked differences.
Students rated GenAI as useful (M=3.63), creativity-enhancing (M=3.66) and intended to keep using it (M=3.92), all significantly above neutral. Overall concerns (M=2.98) did not differ from neutral.
Over-reliance was the highest-rated concern (M=3.66). Concerns about teamwork and social interaction were rated lower.
The authors note the LLM debugging task was used in a high-stakes summative exam with no prior training, which may partly explain the performance gap.

dimensions.authenticity: Frames correcting AI-generated code as a skill students need for AI-augmented development work.
dimensions.capability_verification: Invigilated exam tasks requiring correction of LLM-generated code exposed gaps in debugging and foundational skill.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Authors note the LLM debugging task and the construction tasks measure different cognitive demands, which limits comparability.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Students reported positive views and strong intention to use GenAI, with over-reliance as their main worry; authors call for explicit instruction on GenAI limits.

author_recommendations: Pair instructor-designed tasks with LLM-generated debugging challenges to build error-correction skills gradually (not tested).
Embed explicit instruction on GenAI limitations, biases and ethics, and have students critique and refine AI outputs (not tested).
Use scaffolded, guided integration of GenAI before high-stakes use (not tested).
Institutions should provide professional development and clear policies on integrity, privacy and over-reliance (not tested).
limitations: Two populations from different countries limit generalisability. Study 2 compares tasks with different cognitive demands (debugging vs construction). The design is short-term, and pedagogical integration strategies were not examined (pp. 3180-3181).

quality.note: Clear RQs, appropriate quantitative methods, samples described, and limitations stated. q4 is Unclear: score scales and normalisation between task types are not fully clear (e.g. traditional SDs exceed means), and the task comparison is confounded by task type.

title: Perceived impact of generative AI on assessments: Comparing educator and student perspectives in Australia, Cyprus, and the United States

source_used: Published-version PDF (CC BY-NC) from the University of Sydney repository (ses.library.usyd.edu.au/handle/2123/33787), read in browser via pdf.js text extraction. The PDF could not be saved locally because direct download returned 403. The ScienceDirect route was blocked by CAPTCHA.
ft_reason: HE (three universities); perceived impact of GenAI on assessment and preferences for assessment adaptation are the primary focus; peer reviewed; 2024.
study_design: Cross-sectional international survey with scenario-based items; mixed methods (descriptive/regression analysis plus thematic coding of open responses)

key_findings.finding: Educators and students rated coding assignments and essays as most affected by GenAI (students also rated short-answer and MCQ). Real-time presentations were expected to be least affected.
67% of educators preferred the GenAI-adapted prompt (evaluate or edit ChatGPT output) over the original, against 16% for the original. Students were more divided: 41% adapted, 33% original.

Respondents judged that GenAI availability lowered the original prompts' quality on most of the six dimensions (academic integrity, authenticity, feedback, etc.) and that the adapted prompts recovered this loss.

Educators rated academic integrity slightly more important than the other quality dimensions. Students who preferred the original prompts cited integrity, creativity and original-contribution concerns.
Most respondents expected students to use GenAI to generate whole essays or code; students more often expected help-seeking uses such as ideas, revision and error-checking.

dimensions.integrity_security: Seven-day take-home essays and coding tasks were seen as most exposed; academic integrity was rated the most important dimension by educators.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Authors argue assessment should shift towards evaluation and higher-order thinking, consistent with Bloom's revised taxonomy.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Tested prompts that build ChatGPT use into the task (critique/edit the essay; evaluate generated code and complexity analysis).

Embed evaluative components, such as judging machine-generated content, into revised assessments (not tested).
Design and frame new prompts to centre the process of learning, higher-order thinking and authenticity, so that students see value in them (not tested).
limitations: Non-random voluntary convenience samples that likely over-represent interested respondents; snapshot from spring 2023; variation in disciplines; language issues for Greek-speaking Cypriot participants; no causal inference (Sec 5.3, p. 9). GPT-4 was used to help build codebooks for some open-ended data.

quality.note: Clear RQs; survey built on an established framework (Huber et al.); samples and context described in detail (Table 2); results supported by statistics and coded responses; limitations stated explicitly.

title: ChatGPT versus human essayists: an exploration of the impact of artificial intelligence for authorship and academic integrity in the humanities
authors: T. Revell; Will Yeadon; Glenn Cahilly-Bretzin; I. Clarke; G. Manning; J. Jones; Corinne Mulley; R. J. Pascual; N. Bradley; D. Thomas; Francis Leneghan
source_used: Springer OA PDF (CC BY) from oa_url, saved as pdfs/R54.pdf. Page numbers are article pages (1-19).
ft_reason: HE (first-year English undergraduates, Oxford); academic integrity, detectability and assessment design are primary; GenAI (GPT-4); peer reviewed; 2024. Non-computing discipline.
study_design: Blinded comparative marking study plus AI-detector evaluation, with qualitative analysis of marker comments
discipline: English Language and Literature (Old English poetry commentary)
sample: 68 essays: 28 pre-ChatGPT student commentaries and 40 GPT-4 essays (48 generated, 8 excluded) on 7 Old English passages; marked blind by 7 experienced Oxford markers (text later refers to nine markers in the ICC analysis)
genai_tools: GPT-4 (ChatGPT); detectors GPTZero, Quillbot, ZeroGPT

key_findings.finding: Blind-marked GPT-4 essays averaged about 60.5 against 63.57 for student essays, a difference that was not statistically significant (p about 0.10).
key_findings.location: p. 6, Results; abstract (the abstract gives 60.46, the text 60.48)

key_findings.finding: Markers identified essay origin correctly 79.41% of the time (54/68), but 10 AI essays were judged human, 2 of them as 'definitely human'.

Quillbot (95.59%) and GPTZero (86.76%) beat the human markers and ZeroGPT (64.71%) did worse. The authors stress that only 1.0 precision is acceptable for misconduct, and that mixed human-AI texts were not tested.
AI essays were well structured and formal but described rather than analysed, lacking detailed critical analysis of poetic style and context. Marker agreement was low (ICC about 0.133).

Authors suggest short-term fixes (in-person or invigilated exams, unseen prompts, multimodal questions, rubrics weighted to higher-order thinking) and longer-term redesign (small regular assessments, project and presentation work). They note Oxford's 1-on-1 tutorials make misuse easier to detect.

dimensions.authenticity: Calls for educators to rethink what counts as authentic assessment as AI gets more capable.
dimensions.capability_verification: Finds in-person closed-book unseen exams not yet threatened, while non-invigilated essays are vulnerable; small 1-on-1 tutorials help verify authorship.
dimensions.integrity_security: Neither human markers nor detectors reached the certainty needed for misconduct findings; detectors were not tested on mixed texts.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Proposes reweighting rubrics from organisation and presentation towards higher-order critical analysis.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Demonstrates ethical copiloting (essay planning and idea generation) and the hallucinated references that need expert checking.
dimensions.scalability: Notes Oxford tutorials make misuse easy to spot, but the problem is more urgent in larger seminar settings.
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Raises equity concerns because GPT-4 was a paid service and GPT-3.5 was free.

author_recommendations: Short term: emphasise in-person or invigilated, handwritten, unseen or multimodal tasks (not tested).
Reweight marking rubrics towards detailed critical analysis and higher-order thinking (not tested).
Long term: use small, regular assessments and project, collaborative or presentation work to reduce reliance on final exams (not tested).
Be transparent with staff and students about GenAI capabilities and limitations, and develop an ethical-use framework with stakeholder input (not tested).
limitations: No dedicated limitations section. The authors note test texts were purely AI or purely human (no co-created texts), marker consistency was low, prompt 4 had few essays, and markers' awareness of the study may have caused detection bias. The student essays came from one discipline at one elite institution.

quality.note: Clear aims; blinded design with statistical tests; sample and procedure described with an ethics reference. Minor internal inconsistencies (60.46 vs 60.48; seven vs nine markers). Limitations are only scattered through the text, not set out systematically.

title: Educational Effects of Animated Output and Application-Specific Commands in Programming Classes in the Age of Generative AI
authors: Kazunari Ito
venue: International Conference on Information and Education Technology (ICIET)
ft_reason: Third- and fourth-year undergraduates at a Japanese university (HE); programming assignments designed to be AI-resistant to protect learning and deter copy-paste (assessment design/integrity); GenAI focus; IEEE ICIET conference paper; 2026; English.
study_design: Single-group exploratory case study with an end-of-course Likert questionnaire (13 items) and two open-ended items analysed thematically; no control group
discipline: Programming within an interdisciplinary Social Informatics course (mixed humanities and science majors)
sample: 44 students in one course, April 2025, 11 weeks (7 lessons)
genai_tools: Generative AI services such as ChatGPT (students free to use them in class); Pictogramming web apps with custom commands (JavaScpict, Picthon, Picby, etc.)

key_findings.finding: Assignments used application-specific commands (e.g., pic.RW, pic.M) and animated output. General LLMs are not trained on these, so they tend to produce plausible but non-working code, which forces students to verify and debug.

Most students tried to get complete code from GenAI (A1 mean 4.34), but strongly agreed that it needed modification (A2 mean 4.52). They rated custom commands as effective against copy-paste submissions (B2 mean 4.57, the highest item).
Students reported thinking more deeply (C1 4.39) and better debugging practice (C3 4.18) when AI was less useful. Fairness (C4 3.48) and motivation (B3 3.45) were more divided.
Students agreed AI-resistant tasks were more effective for learning (D1 4.02) but were lukewarm about having more of them in future (D2 3.32). The author reads this as a call for a balanced mix.
Students suggested further designs: self-defined specifications, personal experience, multi-phase changing conditions, explaining the process, and deliberately flawed code to debug.

dimensions.capability_verification: Custom commands make AI output fail, requiring students to show their own debugging and understanding; based on self-report only (Sec II.C, Table V).
dimensions.integrity_security: Students rated custom commands as a strong barrier to naive copy-paste (B2 4.57); no misconduct data collected (Table V).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Argues the design preserves trial-and-error and conceptual learning that copy-paste would bypass (Sec I, Sec II.C).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: AI use was permitted; the author proposes a hybrid model mixing AI-easy and AI-hard tasks to build AI literacy (Sec III.A, Sec IV).
dimensions.workload: Some students appeared to want a lighter, balanced workload, per the gap between D1 and D2 (Sec III.C).
dimensions.feasibility: Relies on an existing purpose-built web environment (Pictogramming series) which other courses would need to have (Sec II).
dimensions.process_visibility: Students suggested asking for explanations of the process leading to a result (Table VII).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Fairness perceptions were divided (C4 3.48; about 60% agreed) (Sec III.C).

author_recommendations: Use application-specific custom commands and animated output to make programming assignments resistant to AI outsourcing (evaluated by student self-report only)
Adopt a hybrid curriculum combining AI-solvable and AI-resistant tasks to build AI literacy (not tested)
Run comparative experiments with control groups and wider age ranges (not tested)

title: Process over Product: A Real-Time, Big Data Approach to Plagiarism Detection via Activity Logs
authors: B S Anurag Rao; Shreya Gurram; Justin Carvalho; Adhithya P S; Animesh Giri
ft_reason: University CS setting (sophomore students; hackathon and in-class assignment); academic integrity (plagiarism detection, including AI-generated code) is the primary focus; GenAI motivation plus LLM-based platform features; EDUCON 2026 peer-reviewed conference; 2026, English. Meets IC1-IC5 on full text.
study_design: System design and evaluation: distributed real-time keystroke-log anomaly detection (unsupervised Isolation Forest) with AST-normalised code-similarity search; synthetic load test plus an in-class evaluation with an honest control group and a group instructed to plagiarise
discipline: Computer science / programming (data structures and algorithms, competitive programming)
sample: Training data: 189 sophomore students in a 3-hour university hackathon (366,987 editing events). Evaluation: 101 sophomore students in a 2-hour in-class assignment (19 honest control, 82 instructed to plagiarise by any means)

key_findings.location: Sec II, Sec IV-B to IV-D, Tables I-II

key_findings.finding: In the in-class evaluation (N = 101), the system had 74 TP, 8 FN, 5 FP and 14 TN: accuracy 87.13%, precision 93.67%, recall 90.24%, F1 91.93%.
Students circumvented copy-paste restrictions as expected; about half of the true positives were manual transcription of AI-generated code, which process monitoring still detected.

False positives were honest students with heavy delete-and-rewrite styles. False negatives were late-stage plagiarism smoothed by earlier honest work; a mass-deletion baseline reset was added after the evaluation but not re-tested.
At submission, the platform also asks LLM-generated multiple-choice questions specific to the student's own code as an extra authorship check (not separately evaluated).

dimensions.capability_verification: Code-specific LLM-generated verification questions at submission are intended to check familiarity with the submitted code (not evaluated) (Sec III).
dimensions.integrity_security: Process-level behavioural monitoring detected most instructed plagiarism attempts, including transcription of AI code, which is presented as a complement or replacement for similarity checkers (Sec V-C, Sec VI).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: LLM hints guide students to the next conceptual step without giving full solutions (Sec III).
dimensions.scalability: Sustained 100 requests per second (each a batch of 150 logs) with 200 concurrent users at about 400 ms latency on 1-vCPU containers; designed for horizontal scaling (Sec V-A).
dimensions.workload: A dashboard with real-time alerts and code replay is meant to support instructor review (Sec IV-G).
dimensions.feasibility: Requires students to work in the custom Superlit web editor; future extensions to VS Code and browser plugins are proposed (Sec VI).
dimensions.process_visibility: Code replay reconstructs how a solution was developed over time and supports evidence-based integrity decisions (Sec IV-G).
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Honest students with atypical iterative styles were falsely flagged; individualised baselines are proposed (Sec V-C, Sec VI).

author_recommendations: Use process-level activity-log monitoring as a complement to, or replacement for, similarity-based detectors (evaluated in one in-class deployment).
Build individualised behavioural baselines per student to reduce false positives (not tested).
Reset behavioural baselines after mass-deletion events to catch late-stage plagiarism (implemented after the evaluation; not tested).
Extend logging to VS Code and competitive-programming platforms, and add error-trajectory signals and an ensemble of models (not tested).
limitations: Authors discuss false positives and negatives and propose fixes (Sec V-C). Also noted: plagiarism was instructed rather than naturally occurring, with an imbalanced 82/19 split; ground truth was confirmed by invigilators using the system's own code-replay feature; single institution and single session; post-evaluation changes not re-tested; no discussion of student privacy, consent or surveillance ethics.

title: Adapting Program Assessment for the Age of Generative AI
authors: Michael P. Verdicchio
ft_reason: Full text confirms HE computing program assessment (ABET) adapted for GenAI, with concrete examples of instruments invalidated by AI and a course-level experience report; IEEE EDUNINE 2025 (peer reviewed); English.
study_design: Position/guidance paper: brief literature summary, program-assessment recommendations, and an experience report from a data structures course with an anonymous student reflection survey (themes generated by ChatGPT)
discipline: Computer science (ABET-accredited program; data structures course); generalised to engineering, technology and computing
sample: Experience report: approximately 30 students completed the project and an anonymous two-prompt reflection survey; pass-rate figures for a code-tracing instrument in 2022 and 2023 (cohort sizes not reported)
genai_tools: ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot

key_findings.finding: Performance indicators, rather than ABET student outcomes, are the best level to adapt for GenAI, e.g., moving from 'implement a solution' to 'validate the correctness of an AI-generated solution' (from code generation toward verification).

An obfuscated code-tracing instrument went from 44% of students meeting the benchmark in 2022 to over 80% in 2023; ChatGPT identified the algorithm despite obfuscation, so that cycle's data was discarded.
An obfuscated deque programming assignment was solved instantly by ChatGPT to 90% of performance requirements, so it was dropped as an assessment instrument.

The replacement multi-part project required a guided design phase and then encouraged GenAI for leaf functions; students who skipped design struggled. Autograders could not be used, so grading relied on rubrics and screencast demos, and rubric scores gave more meaningful outcome data.

Five recommendations: revise performance indicators for GenAI; assessment leaders should check instruments for AI robustness; control the environment (in-class, quiz, exam, paper or computer-based testing); test take-home instruments with ChatGPT/Copilot; design assignments with appropriate professional AI use.

dimensions.authenticity: Recommends assignments where students use GenAI as they would in professional practice (Sec VII, Rec 5).
dimensions.capability_verification: Shows unsupervised instruments can yield misleading outcome-attainment data under AI use (44% to over 80%) (Sec V.B).
dimensions.integrity_security: Obfuscation did not stop ChatGPT; recommends controlled environments and pre-testing take-home tasks against AI tools (Sec V.B; Sec VII).
dimensions.lo_alignment: Adaptation is placed within ABET outcomes, performance indicators and curriculum maps linking instruments to outcomes (Sec III.B; Sec IV; Sec V.A).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: AI encouraged for low-level functions after students design the architecture; students favoured allowing AI by course level and with documentation (Sec VI; Sec VI.B).
dimensions.scalability: Open-ended projects prevented autograding; a standardised API with open architecture is suggested to restore automated testing (Sec VI.A).
dimensions.workload: The only additional instructor burden reported was rubric-based assessment while grading (Sec VI.A).
dimensions.feasibility: Controlled-environment testing is described as a quick, satisfactory solution, especially for smaller schools using paper exams (Sec VII, Rec 3).
dimensions.process_visibility: Design-phase homework deliverables and screencast code tours expose students' process (Sec VI; Sec VI.A).

author_recommendations: Add or revise performance indicators to specify expectations for student GenAI use (not tested)
Assessment leaders should work with instructors to ensure instruments are robust against GenAI (not tested)
Control the assessment environment (in-class, quiz, exam) where suitable (not tested)
Test take-home instruments with ChatGPT and/or GitHub Copilot before use (based on the author's experience)
Design assignments with appropriate professional GenAI use and use them as assessment instruments (experience report only)
limitations: No limitations section. Single-program experience report; the thematic analysis of the student survey was produced by ChatGPT with no reported verification; sample sizes approximate or unreported; the 2022 to 2023 rise is attributed to AI on the basis of the instructor's suspicion and testing, not direct evidence.

quality.note: Full text read. Clear aim; experience-report method; survey analysis delegated to ChatGPT without validation; sample loosely described; no limitations acknowledged.

title: Computing Education in the Era of Generative AI

dimensions.integrity_security: Plagiarism detectors are reported ineffective on AI code and AI use is low-risk compared with contract cheating; secure conditions anticipated.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Questions whether code-writing outcomes remain appropriate; argues code literacy (read, test, verify) stays essential.

dimensions.scalability: Notes LLMs could generate a near-endless supply of novel exercises, reducing the cost of fresh assessment items.

dimensions.accessibility_equity: Notes bias in generated code and comments, and greater access for learners without formal education.

Shift assessment toward judging quality/style across multiple solutions and critiquing AI-generated code (not tested)
Use specification-focused tasks and renewed test-driven development with rewards for incremental testing (not tested)
Teach the wider societal, legal and ethical implications of generative AI (not tested)

title: Online assessment in the age of artificial intelligence

discipline: Mathematics/statistics; upper-level machine learning course with programming (R)

dimensions.capability_verification: Proposes calling students in to explain code that goes beyond the constructs taught.
dimensions.integrity_security: Shows unproctored online exams were heavily compromised; lockdown browsers can be bypassed and malfunction for about 2-3% of students.

Impose strict exam time limits to deter live tutoring (not formally tested)
Screen exam questions with ChatGPT and replace those it answers correctly (not tested)
Require executable code limited to taught constructs, with oral explanation if in doubt (not formally evaluated)

title: Work in Progress: Integration of AI Tools on an Open-Ended Computer Programming Project
authors: Emily Hammond; Courtney J. Faber

author_recommendations: Use timed oral micro-presentations on randomly selected topics in place of take-home writing
Adopt GRE-style adaptive viva questioning so students must prepare across all difficulty levels (not tested)
Structure preparation with Bloom's taxonomy and require students to submit questions and answers before assessments
Modify quizzes with paraphrasing, hand drawings, randomised order and one-at-a-time questions
limitations: Short paper with little methodological detail. The abstract mentions threats to validity, but the text does not discuss them. There is no comparison group, results are aggregate grades only, and feedback is anonymous and informal; the timeframe is inconsistent (two academic years vs four semesters); one figure is ambiguous ('80% ... (83%)'); the author acknowledges using GenAI to condense the paper and generate Table 1.

quality.note: RQs are stated, but methods, data collection and analysis are thin, conclusions about improved comprehension and ethical AI use rest on aggregate grades and informal feedback, and no limitations are given in the text.

title: Assessing Student Proficiency in Foundational Developer Tools Through Live Checkoffs
authors: Connor McMahon; Lauren Feldman
venue: Proceedings of the 57th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education V.1 (SIGCSE TS 2026), St. Louis, MO, USA
ft_reason: Undergraduate CS course (IC1); the paper is about designing and running a live one-on-one assessment format (IC2); GenAI's ability to complete take-home work is given as a stated reason for in-person checkoffs that verify authentic skill (IC3, though AI is a motivating rationale rather than an object of study); peer-reviewed SIGCSE TS experience report (IC4); 2026, English (IC5).
study_design: Experience report with descriptive quantitative data (scores, optional post-checkoff surveys, queue/duration logs) and informal TA feedback
discipline: Computer science (Systems Fundamentals course)
level: Undergraduate (third required course in the CS major)
sample: 237 enrolled students across two sections, Spring 2025; survey responses 139-168 per checkoff (Tables 4-5); TA feedback from weekly staff meetings
genai_tools: Generic GenAI only (no specific tool named; no AI used in the assessment)

key_findings.finding: Three live checkoffs (CLI, debugger, Git) had students demonstrate tool use and verbally explain concepts to a TA using scripted questions and a standardised rubric; the authors present this as a way to verify authentic proficiency when GenAI can complete take-home work.
Most students reached baseline proficiency: median first-attempt scores were full marks on all three checkoffs (CLI mean 15.31/16, debugger 14.55/15, Git 43.62/44).

Most survey respondents agreed or strongly agreed that preparing for and completing the checkoff improved their skills (88% CLI, 85% debugging, 93% Git), and students reported more office-hours use and a stronger sense of community.

Checkoffs ran longer than planned (median 9.5, 19 and 25 min against 5, 15 and 15 min anticipated), demand peaked on the last day, and checkoff appointments took up about 80% of TA office-hour time; switching to booked appointments with a time limit and pair format reduced queue time.
key_findings.location: Table 6; Sec 6.2.4; Sec 6.4.1; Sec 7 TA Staffing

key_findings.finding: No integrity violations were observed, but the authors recognise question-sharing risk and plan multiple versions of each checkoff.

dimensions.authenticity: Checkoffs are run in the real tool environments students will use and resemble technical interviews, which the authors argue is more authentic than written exams.
dimensions.capability_verification: Live demonstration plus verbal explanation lets TAs probe understanding and confirm individual baseline proficiency.
dimensions.integrity_security: In-person format is positioned as verifying authentic skill in the GenAI era; question sharing is noted as a residual risk to be handled with multiple versions.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Skills assessed are listed per checkoff and the debugger checkoff was scoped to tool use rather than real-time bug finding to match the learning objectives.
dimensions.scalability: Ran with 237 students using TAs in office hours; authors call it scalable but report long queues and overrun durations.
dimensions.workload: Checkoff appointments consumed about 80% of TA office-hour time; authors advise avoiding other large deadlines in checkoff week.
dimensions.feasibility: Docker containers, scripts and rubrics standardised delivery; environment setup problems and last-day demand caused bottlenecks.
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Two attempts per question and a full redo reduced stress; a quieter space is recommended for students with accommodations.

author_recommendations: Use appointment-based scheduling with sign-ups closed the week before and a time limit for all checkoffs
Create multiple versions of each checkoff to reduce question sharing (not tested)
Raise checkoff weighting to 15% of the course grade and apply a small penalty to second attempts (not tested)
Avoid large assignment deadlines during checkoff week to manage TA and student workload
Offer students with accommodations a quieter space (not tested)
limitations: Single course and single semester; checkoffs were low stakes (1-2% of grade) in this offering; survey was optional and self-reported; ceiling effects in scores; TA feedback was informal; GenAI impact was not measured; no formal limitations section.

quality.note: Clear experience report with descriptive data that supports its claims; limitations are only implicit in challenges and lessons learned, with no dedicated limitations section.

title: Generative AI in Programming Education: An Empirical Analysis of Student Performance and Assessment Challenges in the LLM Era
authors: Suyang Zhu; Zhengtao Liu
venue: 2026 International Conference on Big Data and Informatization Education (ICBDIE 2026), Beijing, China (ACM)
ft_reason: Undergraduate computing courses (IC1); compares assignment versus invigilated exam performance and argues output-only grading is no longer valid, proposing assessment reform (IC2); LLM use is central (IC3); ACM conference paper (IC4); 2026, English (IC5).
study_design: Longitudinal mixed-method observational study across three semesters (questionnaires, lab observation, LMS code-submission data, invigilated exam scores), with pre/post comparison around early 2025
discipline: Computer science / AI (NLP, Data Mining, Python Programming)
sample: 412 undergraduates across five course offerings (Table 1); 89 pre-watershed questionnaire responses; 3,524 assignment submissions (Table 2); exam comparison of 218 students in NLP and Python courses (Table 4)
genai_tools: DeepSeek, Doubao (Dola), ChatGPT, Ernie, Qwen, others; AI-assisted IDEs such as Cursor counted under their underlying model

key_findings.finding: Frequent use of AI coding assistants rose from 4.5% of the pre-watershed cohort to 89.5% post-watershed, with DeepSeek and Doubao replacing ChatGPT as the main tools.
AI-generated assignment submissions scored higher than self-written ones (mean score rate 0.803 vs 0.644, p < .01) but were submitted only marginally earlier (normalised time 0.855 vs 0.872).

In invigilated closed-book exams with LLMs prohibited, AI-reliant students performed the same as self-sufficient students (0.630 vs 0.632), which the authors interpret as competency hollowing and evidence that assignment output no longer validly measures ability.

Failures in AI-generated code were mostly API/library misuse (55.9%) and logic errors (43.4%) rather than syntax errors (0.7%), indicating a shift in student effort towards verification and debugging.

Authors propose process-oriented assessment (oral code defence with no credit for unexplained AI code, Git commit-history tracking), reverse-engineering tasks on flawed AI code, and a 3-layer No-AI / AI-assisted / manual-validation curriculum.

dimensions.authenticity: Proposes reviewer-style tasks (correcting flawed AI code) as matching the new cognitive role of programmers, but does not evaluate them.
dimensions.capability_verification: Invigilated exams showed no ability gain for AI-reliant students despite higher assignment marks, so the authors argue only controlled or process-based assessment verifies capability.
dimensions.integrity_security: Treats output-only grading of take-home assignments as compromised by ubiquitous LLM use and says bans are futile.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Argues output-based mean-score grading is no longer a valid proxy for computational-thinking outcomes.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Recommends staged AI permission, from No-AI foundations to AI-assisted projects to manual validation of AI code (not tested).
dimensions.process_visibility: Recommends Git commit-history review and oral code defence to make the process visible (not tested).

author_recommendations: Mandatory oral code defence; no credit for AI-generated functions the student cannot explain (not tested)
Git-based process tracking to distinguish incremental commits from single large AI-code commits (not tested)
Reverse-engineering tasks in which students find, explain and fix errors in flawed AI-generated solutions (not tested)
3-layer course structure: No-AI zones for the first 4-6 weeks, then open AI-assisted projects, then constrained manual validation and refactoring of AI code (not tested)
limitations: No limitations section. Single-instructor, single-institution observational data with non-equivalent cohorts and different courses pre and post; pre-watershed usage based on 89 voluntary questionnaires while post-watershed relied on mandatory disclosure; AI-reliant versus self-written classification is self-reported; the Table 4 standard deviations (0.131/0.109) do not match those in the text (0.167/0.171); a t-test is reported for proportions; confounds such as course difficulty are not addressed.

quality.note: Sample and data sources are well described, but the cohort comparison is confounded, some statistics are inconsistent between table and text, and limitations are not acknowledged.
